 “(California Government Code Section 54954.3).
 (a) Every agenda for regular meetings shall provide an opportunity for members of the
 public to directly address the legislative body on any item of interest to the public, before
 or during the legislative body’s consideration of the item, that is within the subject matter
 jurisdiction of the legislative body, provided that no action shall be taken on any item not
 appearing on the agenda unless the action is otherwise authorized by subdivision (b) of

City Council  Tuesday, March 18, 2025
  Section 54954.2 [section omitted].

 (b) (1) The legislative body of a local agency may adopt reasonable regulations to ensure
 that the intent of the subdivision (a) is carried out, including, but not limited to, regulations
 limiting the total amount of time allocated for public testimony on particular issues and for
 each individual speaker.
  (2) Notwithstanding paragraph (1), when the legislative body of a local agency limits
 time for public comment, the legislative body of a local agency shall provide at least twice
 the allotted time to a member of the public who utilizes a translator to ensure that non-
 English speakers receive the same opportunity to directly address the legislative body of
 a local agency.”

 In furtherance of Section 54954.3 of the Brown Act, the public is allotted to speak a total
 of two (2) minutes on the entirety of the Consent Calendar, Appointment(s), New
 Business and Closed Session, with two (2) minutes on each Public Hearing, and, if
 desired, an additional two (2) minutes on items not on the agenda that are within the
 subject matter jurisdiction of the City Council. As specified in the Brown Act, a speaker
 utilizing a translator will receive twice the amount of time specified.

DATE:  MARCH 18, 2025

TO:  HONORABLE MAYOR AND CITY COUNCIL

FROM:  ECONOMIC AND COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT DEPARTMENT
  PLANNING DIVISION

DISTRICT:  ALL

SUBJECT:  RECEIVE THE SUMMARY OF THE 2024 ANNUAL HOUSING
  ELEMENT PROGRESS REPORT

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends that the City Council:

  1. Receive the summary of the 2024 Annual Housing Element Progress Report; and,

  2. Direct staff to file the report with the California Department of Housing and
  Community Development (HCD).

BACKGROUND

Government Code Section 65400 requires that all California cities provide an Annual
Housing Element Progress Report to the Governor’s Office of Planning and Research
(OPR) and the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD).
The intent of the statute is to describe the City’s progress in meeting its share of the
Regional Housing Needs Assessment (RHNA). Also, by filing this report with OPR and
HCD, the City may be eligible for future housing grants.

DISCUSSION

A total of 6,640 units were allocated to the City of Palmdale during the 6th cycle RHNA
allocation plan, which covers the planning period October 2021 through October 2029.
These units are distributed by affordability level, and the Housing Element of the General
Plan must identify how the City plans to accommodate them. The City is required to
designate land for housing to ensure that there is enough residentially designated land to
meet its RHNA allocation. However, it is not required to ensure units are built. The City is
required to report on the progress of housing development in the form of the Annual
Housing Element Progress Report.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Receive the summary of 2024 Annual Housing Element Report
March 18, 2025
Page 2

In April 2023, the City adopted Zoning Ordinance Amendment 21-007, updating Title 17
of the Palmdale Municipal Code to be consistent with Palmdale 2045, the City’s adopted
General Plan. This update included additional land use designations that allow flexibility
in multi-family and mixed-use zones for residential development.

For the calendar year 2024, 151 housing units were issued a building permit. The table
below provides a breakdown of housing units per year from 2021 to 2024.

SUBJECT:  ADOPT RESOLUTION NO. CC 2025-019, A RESOLUTION OF THE
  CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF PALMDALE, APPROVING A
  MODIFICATION OF THE PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING
  TIME FROM 7:00 PM TO 5:00 PM BEGINNING AT THE APRIL 10,
  2025

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

Adopt Resolution No. CC 2025-019, approving a modification of the Planning
Commission meeting time from 7:00 pm to 5:00 pm beginning at the April 10, 2025,
meeting.

BACKGROUND

Palmdale Municipal Code (PMC) Section 2.46.070 states that "meetings of the Planning
Commission shall be held on such days and at such time and location as may be
established by the Commission for the conduct of its business and ratified by the City
Council.” On June 3, 2009, the City Council adopted Resolution No. CC 2009-093 to
modify the Planning Commission meetings from two meetings per month on the second
and fourth Thursday to one meeting per month, held on the second Thursday of the
month. The Planning Commission of the City of Palmdale currently convenes on the
second Thursday of each month at 7:00 pm in the Council Chamber of the City of
Palmdale located at 38300 North Sierra Highway, Suite B.

On February 13, 2025, the Planning Commission adopted Resolution No. PC-2025-004
recommending City Council approval to modify the Planning Commission meeting time
from 7:00 pm to 5:00 pm (see attached Resolution).
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Resolution No. CC 2025-019
March 18, 2025
Page 2

DISCUSSION

Planning Commission meetings are a platform to conduct the City’s corporate business
affairs with various businesses and the development community. To be consistent with
the City Council meeting time, staff recommends modifying the Planning Commission
meeting time from 7:00 pm to 5:00 pm.

Modifying the time allows the Planning Commission to conduct City business during hours
that align with the corporate, development, legislative, and business community. This will
allow the Commission, staff, businesses, and community to conduct business during
standard working hours instead of late into the evening, which can negatively affect health
and wellbeing and lead to decisions being compromised due to fatigue.

FISCAL IMPACT

$0; There is no fiscal impact associated with this action.

STRATEGIC PLAN

Goal II: Ensure long-term fiscal health of the City and maintain funding for services.

  A. Involve and expand engagement to enhance public oversight and transparency.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Award and Approve Agreement No. A-8679 with Mendoza Engineering Company,
  Inc., for construction services for PN 862, Marie Kerr Swim Deck Expansion
  Project for a not to exceed amount of $340,736, which includes a contract amount
  of $309,760 plus a 10% contingency amount of $30,976 for a term of 50 working
  days from the date of the Notice to Proceed; and,

  2. Authorize the City Manager or her designee to execute the Agreement No. A-
  8679 with Mendoza Engineering Company, Inc., including minimal and/or non-
  substantial changes.

BACKGROUND

Project No. 862 will expand the Marie Kerr Pool facility deck to increase capacity and
expand operations. The project will move existing fencing and install new fencing,
including a new extended patio deck to improve ingress/egress routes. The added deck
space will allow for expanded swim team operations, additional space for family
members to watch, and a handicapped-accessible walk path and entry connecting to
the adjacent recreation center. The project will also include modification of drainage
infrastructure, new landscaping and irrigation, installation of facility and path lighting,
and resurfacing of the existing pool deck surfaces. The City was awarded a grant for the
 Report to Mayor and City Council

construction of the pool deck by the Los Angeles County Regional Park and Open Space
District (RPOSD) in June 2023.

The project was delayed due to the Los Angeles County Health Department plan review
process. After the plans were approved, the City finalized the design with JT Engineering
and prepared construction bid documents.

DISCUSSION

On August 21, 2024, the project was advertised for construction bids electronically
through Planet Bids with five (5) vendors registered as prime contractors. On September
25, 2024, two (2) bids for this project were received, summarized, and listed below:

responsive bidder.

FISCAL IMPACT

$340,736; This project is funded using Los Angeles County Regional Park and Open
Space District (RPOSD) Measure A grant funds. The $340,736 cost includes a 10%
contingency of $30,976.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Approve the Amended and Restated Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) of the
  Antelope Valley RWMG IRWMP cost-sharing Agreement No. A- 6389, for a not to
  exceed amount of $16,923 and extend the term of the agreement through January
  2027; and,

  2. Authorize the City Manager or her designee to execute the Amended and
  Restated MOU of the Antelope Valley RWMG IRWMG cost-sharing Agreement
  No. A- 6389.

BACKGROUND

The City became involved in the RWMG in 2007 to pursue grant funding and facilitate the
implementation of the IRWMP, which was adopted by the City in 2008. An update of the
IRWMP is needed to identify Antelope Valley region water management issues, update
current supply and demand projections, and comply with the Department of Water
Resources guidelines for grant eligibility. The amended and restated MOU sets forth the
funding to be provided by each of the eleven (11) parties of the RWMG.

The Antelope Valley RWMG is composed of Antelope Valley-East Kern Water Agency,
Palmdale Water District, Quartz Hill Water District, Littlerock Creek Irrigation District,
Antelope Valley State Contractors Association, City of Palmdale, City of Lancaster,
County Sanitation District No. 14 of Los Angeles County, County Sanitation District No.

DISCUSSION

The Amended and Restated MOU of the Antelope Valley RWMG cost sharing Agreement
No. A-6389 is to conform to the requirements of the adopted IRWMP. The funding shall
be used to cover costs incurred by the RWMG for ongoing regional stakeholder meetings,
IRWMP project updates, and grant support. Additionally, the MOU confirms the intent of
the parties to continue to fund twenty-five percent (25%) of the United States Geological
Survey Groundwater Monitoring Program (USGS Program) through September 2026.

Several agencies already have stormwater-related projects in mind, including the City’s
Avenue R regional basin project, the City of Lancaster storm drain infrastructure project,

consultant to prepare a “Mini Update” of the Plan to comply with the 2016 Guidelines.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Approve the First Amendment to Agreement No. A-8233, with MNS Engineers,
  Inc. (MNS) for project management services for PN 669, 10th Street West
  Widening, increasing the agreement by $227,000 for a total not to exceed amount
  of $418,000 with an extension of 22 months for a total term of 45 months; and,

  2. Authorize the City Manager or her designee to execute the First Amendment to
  Agreement No. A-8233 with MNS Engineers, Inc., including minimal and/or non-
  substantial changes.

BACKGROUND

On March 1, 2023, the City Council approved Agreement No. A-8233 with MNS, for
project management services for PN 669, 10th Street West Widening Project at SR14.
10th Street West is a major north-south corridor in the City, providing access to the
adjacent businesses including the Antelope Valley Mall. The project is currently in the
final design stage with substantial work completed by AECOM. The outstanding work
includes final design drawings and specifications, permitting, constructability review,
funding partners approvals, Caltrans permitting, and right-of-way acquisition. This project
will improve the level of service by increasing capacity, reducing congestion, and
improving overall operations and safety along 10th Street West, including its access to the
Antelope Valley Mall and the Sierra Commons Shopping Area.

DISCUSSION

The proposed First Amendment to Agreement No. A-8233 extends MNS’ project
management services for the 10th Street West Widening Project, ensuring the timely
delivery of the project through the bidding phase and addressing outstanding design and
permitting requirements.

MNS will continue to act as the City’s representative for this project, providing the
following key services:

    Project Management: Oversee the finalization of design and bidding documents
  to ensure compliance with City standards, funding guidelines, and permitting
  requirements. The consultant will coordinate with City staff, review the bid package
  prepared by AECOM, and facilitate communication between the City and
  regulatory agencies such as Caltrans.
    Right-of-Way (R/W) Documentation: Document existing private property
  conditions affected by R/W acquisitions using drone video footage. This
  documentation will establish a clear pre-construction record to mitigate disputes or
  claims related to property damage.

The proposed amendment is needed to help complete the final design, permits, and
bidding for the 10th Street West Widening project. Although progress has been made,
there are still tasks to finish, such as finalizing design drawings, working with SCE on
facility relocations, obtaining approvals, completing right-of-way acquisitions, and
addressing challenges with utility relocations. Extending MNS' contract will ensure
continued project management and help complete these tasks efficiently while meeting
City standards and funding requirements. This amendment will provide the resources
needed to keep the project moving forward and smoothly into the construction phase.

R grants. Sufficient funds are budgeted and available in FY 2024-25.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Approve Second Amendment to Agreement No. A-8470 with MNS
  Engineers, Inc. (MNS), for construction management and inspection
  services for PN 795, Sam Yellen Park Phase 2 project, increasing the
  agreement by $133,640, for the total not to exceed amount of $720,208 with
  an extension of six months for a total of 22 months; and,

  2. Authorize the City Manager or her designee to execute the Second
  Amendment to Agreement No. A-8470 with MNS, including minimal and/or
  non-substantive changes.

BACKGROUND

On August 22, 2023, the City Council awarded and approved Agreement No. A-8470
with MNS for professional services for the Sam Yellen Park Phase 2 project for
$535,568 for 16 months. The First Amendment was executed on February 7, 2025,
with additional services, extending the contract term 6 months, and increasing the
contract price by $51,000 for a revised contract amount not to exceed $586,568. Due
to the project work size, existing site condition, and additional work, an outside
consultant firm was required. The scope of work includes construction management,
quality control, and project inspection.
 Report to Mayor and City Council

DISCUSSION

MNS will provide construction inspection services to the City to monitor the
contractor’s ongoing work. The inspector will prepare punch lists, oversee the work,
and ensure quality control.

MNS will also offer construction support, including meetings with the contractor as
needed, handling project close-out, managing contractors’ claims, and overseeing day-
to-day project management activities.

Because of current staff limitations in providing full-time inspection across multiple
trades, MNS was selected to assist with these construction inspection services.

   City Council Staff Report
DATE:  MARCH 18, 2025

TO:  HONORABLE MAYOR AND CITY COUNCIL

FROM:  PUBLIC WORKS DEPARTMENT
  INNOVATION AND ENVIRONMENTAL DIVISION

DISTRICT:  ALL

SUBJECT:  APPROVE EXPANSION OF THE POWER CHOICE SOLAR AND
  BATTERY PROGRAM AND THE FIRST AMENDMENT TO THE
  POWER CHOICE PROGRAM MANAGEMENT AGREEMENT

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Approve expansion of the Power Choice Solar and Battery Program;

  2. Approve the First Amendment to the Power Choice Program Management
  Agreement No. A-8538; and,

  3. Authorize the City Manager or her designee to execute the First Amendment to
  the Power Choice Program Management Agreement No. A-8538.

BACKGROUND

The City’s Community Choice Aggregation (CCA) Program, Energy for Palmdale’s
Independent Choice (EPIC), was established by the City Council through the adoption
of Resolution No. CC 2018-087, approving the submittal of an Implementation Plan
(Plan) in accordance with Public Utilities Code Section 366.2(c) on December 4, 2018.
The Plan was certified by the Energy Division on February 28, 2019, and EPIC
successfully began serving customers on October 1, 2022.

In addition to providing our customers with renewable energy at competitive prices,
EPIC intends to offer customer programs to support the state’s renewable energy goals
by leveraging innovation and cutting-edge technologies, enhancing grid stability, and
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Approve First Amendment Agrmt No. A-8538
March 18, 2025
Page 2

creating new meaningful benefits for our residents. The actions before the City Council
support this effort.

On November 11, 2023, CalChoice and Participate.Energy, LLC, introduced the EPIC
Power Choice Program to the City Council, a collaborative initiative with Tesla designed
to offer Palmdale’s EPIC customers a residential solar and battery storage solution. The
City Council formally adopted this program through a series of agreements, establishing
an accessible path for the community to acquire solar panels and battery storage without
upfront costs or credit checks.

The EPIC Power Choice Program empowers residents with the benefits of solar energy,
including lower energy costs, backup power, and the opportunity to participate in grid
services, making clean energy more equitable and accessible for all. The program
officially launched to all residential customers on May 16, 2024.

DISCUSSION

The Power Choice Program promotes solar market accessibility by eliminating credit
checks, requiring no upfront costs, and offering low energy rates. In the past, similar
programs were limited to individuals with high credit scores, restricting solar benefits to
those who could afford the systems. Initially available only to residential customers, there
is a proposal to expand the program to include all commercial and industrial customers.
Given the program's significant benefits, staff recommend increasing marketing efforts to
ensure that all Palmdale residents and businesses know and can take advantage of this
valuable opportunity through EPIC, improving access to energy savings and resilience
for the entire community.

EPIC Power Choice for Commercial and Industrial Customers

Due to the success of the residential program, City staff are requesting the City Council’s
approval to create a similar model for commercial and industrial customers. This new
program will help remove financial barriers to installing solar for businesses, providing
them with an additional option to access the benefits of solar and battery storage. The
commercial and industrial parts of the EPIC Power Choice program will be designed like
the residential program, offering no upfront costs and fully financed systems for 25 years.
Each system will be custom-designed to maximize energy and cost savings for local
businesses.

EPIC Power Choice Marketing Efforts Expansion

Since launching the EPIC Power Choice Program, staff have conducted various
marketing activities to boost participation. These efforts include a targeted social media
campaign across the City’s platforms to raise awareness, promoting the program through
City and EPIC newsletters, and attending public events to encourage participation among
EPIC customers.

Expanding the program to include Channel Partners offers an opportunity to enhance its
impact by increasing marketing efforts. This will involve a dedicated sales force to
promote the program more strategically. Staff and Participate.Energy LLC, propose
engaging Channel Partners to raise program awareness, provide customers with more
options, and increase participation by encouraging competition among installers. With this
approach, Palmdale residents and businesses can choose from local and regional
installers offering consistent solar and battery specifications. Since all Channel Partners
will follow the same program policies and pricing, customers can easily compare offers
and select the best option.

The existing EPIC Power Choice program will remain available to customers who wish to
participate directly with Tesla through the EPIC or Tesla website. Adding Channel
Partners will help increase marketing and outreach efforts while offering the City’s
residents more choices.

The Power Choice Program involves several agreements between the program partners
(i.e., the City and Participate.Energy, LLC) and the program participants (i.e., EPIC
customers). These agreements define the roles, responsibilities, costs, and the operation
and maintenance of the program, including the following:

Program Management Agreement (PMA)

The PMA includes a scope of services generally provided by the City. These services
include marketing and outreach to customers in the EPIC service territory to promote
the program and encourage program participation. The PMA Amendment modifies the
existing scope of services to add services to be performed by Participate.Energy, LLC
strengthens and augments the marketing and outreach services provided by City staff.

These additional services will be conducted under the guidance and direction of City
staff.

Per the Amendment, compensation for these services will be based on a minimal “per
watt” installed for each system that has reached operational status. This fee will be
subtracted from the current PMA fee per watt installed that reached completion and
operation status. The average fee for a residential system is $380 per home.

The Framework Agreement

The Framework Agreement, which also includes the Channel Partner Agreements, details
the structure of the agreement between the City and Participate.Energy LLC, and
describes each partner’s responsibilities.

Under the proposed program, the different partners would hold the following
responsibilities:

    Participate.Energy LLC, is the financier responsible for funding, procuring, and
  managing the Power Choice Program, including ongoing operations.
    The City, through EPIC, will lend its creditworthiness to pursue an equitable
  process by ensuring that program participation is not subject to individual credit
  approvals. Additionally, EPIC will purchase the energy generated from solar and
  battery equipment and sell said energy to the program participants at a competitive
  rate. Finally, EPIC will support the program partners by marketing the Power
  Choice Program to Palmdale residents.

FISCAL IMPACT

$0; This action has no fiscal impact on the General Fund. The current program design
calls for the City to collect a fee of $0.40 per watt during the construction phase in
connection with the required development services. However, with Participate.Energy,
LLC, added efforts to boost participation through the Channel Partners program, this fee
will be adjusted to $0.35 per watt. Additionally, the City will continue to receive the
agreed revenue streams, including a service fee of $0.02 per kilowatt-hour (kWh)
generated and a monthly fee of $15.00 for each installed Powerwall sustained
throughout the program’s duration.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

Adopt Resolution No. CC 2025-024, a Resolution of the City Council of the City of
Palmdale granting authority to the City Manager to enter into certain contracts on behalf
of EPIC and rescinding and replacing Section 5 of Resolution No. CC 2019-042.

BACKGROUND

The City’s Community Choice Aggregation (CCA) Program, EPIC, was established by
the City Council by adopting Resolution No. CC 2018-087, approving the submittal of
an Implementation Plan (Plan), in accordance with Public Utilities Code Section
366.2(c), on December 4, 2018.

The Plan was certified by the Energy Division on February 28, 2019, and EPIC
successfully began serving customers on October 1, 2022. The actions before the City
Council are in support of this effort.

On April 2, 2019, the City Council adopted Resolution No. 2019-042, authorizing the City
to become a party to the California Choice Energy Authority (CalChoice) Joint Exercise
Powers of Authority. It authorized the execution of an Administrative Services Agreement
with CalChoice. CalChoice provides a suite of services, including energy portfolio
management and the negotiation of energy supply agreements on behalf of EPIC,

including those contracts that ensure EPIC meets its various state-mandated
procurement obligations.

DISCUSSION

Because timely action is essential in certain energy contracting situations, Resolution No.
2019-042 granted procurement authority to the City Manager for specific contracts. Staff
now recommend that the City Council expand this authority to include certain
procurements required by the CPUC that are unlikely to raise policy concerns and do not
need City Council approval before execution.

CCA programs allow residents and businesses to purchase electricity from local
government agencies and give local governments the authority to manage energy
resources on behalf of their communities and customers. CCAs can provide their
communities with many environmental, social, and economic benefits. Central to the
concept of CCA is local choice. It allows communities to decide about their energy
resources and investments within their area and beyond. It also will enable communities
to reinvest locally in programs that support economic, social, and environmental justice
goals. Over 200 towns, cities, and counties serve over eleven million customers through
community choice energy programs.

EPIC energy agreements and contracting are often time-sensitive, requiring swift execution.
Therefore, it is appropriate for EPIC executive management to have the discretion to
execute certain power supply contracts. City Council adopted Resolution No. 2019-042,
which, grants certain procurement authority to the City Manager.

The City Council seeks to modify and expand the granted authority to include CPUC-
mandated procurements unlikely to raise policy concerns requiring prior approval.

FISCAL IMPACT

Based on the proposed rate schedule, anticipated revenues generated will be sufficient
to cover EPIC’s costs of the program.

Staff recommend that the City Council:

BACKGROUND

In August 2021, the City Council adopted Resolution No. CC 2021-071, designating
Knorr, as a sole source provider for aquatic facility equipment and services. Knorr is an
authorized service provider recognized by our equipment manufacturers and is well
known for providing industry-leading service, equipment, and support.

On October 5, 2022, the City entered into an agreement with Knorr to provide all aquatic
mechanical system inspections, maintenance, and repair for pools at McAdam, Oasis,
Marie Kerr, Courson, and DryTown Water Park.

DISCUSSION

Maintaining the aquatic infrastructure is crucial to ensuring the safe and uninterrupted
operation of City pools and DryTown Waterpark. Delays in inspections, preventive
maintenance, or repairs could disrupt operations, negatively affect the guest experience,
and increase the likelihood of costly emergency repairs.

Additional funds are required to fulfill the remainder of the contract term, as all allocated
funds have already been expended. Repair services must proceed without interruption
to meet existing repair needs and maintain the ongoing functionality of the aquatic
mechanical systems. Preventive maintenance schedules, past wear patterns, and
projected future repairs have been used to estimate the funds required to complete the
contract term.

FISCAL IMPACT

$596,000; Funds are budgeted in Contract Services, Maintenance, and Repair accounts
in Facilities Maintenance and DryTown Water Park divisions. Sufficient funds were
adopted for Fiscal Year 24/25. Future funding will be proposed and approved through
the annual budget process.

Access/Circulation

Street improvements will be constructed along the project frontage on Avenue S and
provide two access points to the site. The City Engineer and the Los Angeles County Fire
Department have reviewed the project and confirmed that it is designed to provide safe
vehicular access and flow.

Operations

The fueling station and grocery store will operate 24 hours a day and have between three
and five employees for each eight-hour shift. Security cameras will be installed, and
access will be shared with the Palmdale Sheriff's Station.

ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW

Pursuant to the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), an Initial Study was
prepared to determine whether the project would have a significant effect on the
environment. The Initial Study analyzed the potential for environmental impacts, and all
topics were found to have either no impact, a less than significant impact, or a less than
significant impact with mitigation incorporated. Mitigation measures for biological
resources, cultural resources, geology/soils, noise, and tribal cultural resources were
included to reduce impacts to a less than significant level. As such, an MND and MMRP
were prepared and circulated in accordance with CEQA Guidelines.

FISCAL IMPACT

$26,063.11; Revenues in the amount of $26,063.11 reflect the fees paid by the applicant
associated with applying. Approval of the proposed project facilitates future construction
of a convenience store and fueling station on a vacant parcel which will increase
revenue from property tax and sales tax once construction is complete.

   1 INTRODUCTION
  Introduction
  Preface
This Initial Study/Mitigated Negative Declaration (IS/MND) has been prepared to evaluate potential
environmental effects resulting from the proposed Maverik Fueling Station Project located north of
Avenue S and approximately 180 feet west of SR-14, in the city of Palmdale, County of Los Angeles.
California. The proposed Project is located on Assessor Parcel Number (APN) 3004-016-032.

As established in State of California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) Guidelines Section §15063(c),
the purposes of an IS/MND are to:

  •  Provide the Lead Agency with information to use as the basis for deciding whether to
  prepare an Environmental Impact Report (EIR), Negative Declaration (ND), or Mitigated
  Negative Declaration (MND);
  •  Enable an applicant or Lead Agency to modify a project, mitigating adverse impacts before
  an EIR is prepared, thereby enabling the project to qualify for an ND or MND;
  •  Assist in the preparation of an EIR, if one is required;
  •  Facilitate environmental assessment early in the design of a project;
  •  Provide a factual basis for finding in an ND or MND that a project will not have a significant
  effect on the environment;
  •  Eliminate unnecessary EIRs; and,
  •  Determine whether a previously prepared EIR could be used with the project.

This Initial Study/Mitigated Negative Declaration (IS/MND) has evaluated each of the issue areas
contained in the CEQA Checklist, as provided in Section 3.0 of this document. The objective of this
environmental document is to inform the City decision‐makers, representatives of other
affected/responsible agencies, and other interested parties of the potential environmental effects that
may be associated with the proposed Project.

This IS/MND therefore serves as the environmental review of the proposed Project, as required
pursuant to Title 14, Division 6, Chapter 3 of the State of California Code of Regulations for
implementation of CEQA and the Public Resources Code (PRC) §21000, et seq.

  Regulatory Guidance
An IS/MND is prepared by a lead agency to determine if a project may have a significant effect on the
environment. In accordance with the CEQA Guidelines, Section §15064, an EIR must be prepared if the
Initial Study (IS) indicates that the proposed project under review may have a potentially significant
impact on the environment. A negative declaration may be prepared instead, if the lead agency
prepares a written statement describing the reasons why a proposed Project would not have a
significant effect on the environment, and, therefore, why it does not require the preparation of an EIR
(CEQA Guidelines Section §15371). According to CEQA Guidelines Section §15070, a Negative

Declaration/Mitigated Negative Declaration shall be prepared for a project subject to CEQA when
either:

(a) The Initial Study shows there is no substantial evidence, in light of the whole record before the
agency, that the proposed Project may have a significant effect on the environment, or

(b) The Initial Study identified potentially significant effects, but:

(1) Revisions in the project plans or proposals made by or agreed to by the applicant before the
proposed negative declaration is released for public review would avoid the effects or mitigate the
effects to a point where clearly no significant effects would occur; and,

2) There is no substantial evidence, in light of the whole record before the agency, that the proposed
project as revised may have a significant effect on the environment. If revisions are adopted into the
proposed project in accordance with the CEQA Guidelines Section 15070(b), a Mitigated Negative
Declaration is prepared.

  Lead Agency
The lead agency is the public agency with primary responsibility over a proposed project. Where two
or more public agencies are to be involved with a project, State CEQA Guidelines Section §15051
provides criteria for identifying the lead agency. Specifically, State CEQA Guidelines §15051(b) states:

(b) If the project is to be carried out by a nongovernmental person or entity, the lead agency shall be
the public agency with the greatest responsibility for supervising or approving the project as a whole.

(1) The lead agency will normally be the agency with the general governmental powers, such as a city
of county, rather than an agency with a single or limited purpose such as an air pollution control district
or a district which will provide public serve or public utility to the project.

Since the proposed project is located in the City of Palmdale, County of Los Angeles, pursuant to PRC
Code Section §21067, and State CEQA Guidelines §15367, The City of Palmdale is the Lead Agency for
this proposed project. As the Lead Agency, therefore, the City is responsible for the review and approval
of the proposed project. Based on the findings of the IS for the project, The City of Palmdale has
determined that a MND is the appropriate environmental document to prepare in compliance with
CEQA (California PRC Section §21000 et seq.). As stated under CEQA Section §21064.5, an MND may
be prepared for a project subject to CEQA when an IS has identified no potentially significant effects
on the environment. The purpose of the MND and the IS checklist is to determine any potentially
significant impacts associated with the proposed project and to incorporate mitigation measures into
the project design as necessary to reduce or eliminate the significant or potentially significant effects
of the project.

This IS/MND has been prepared for the proposed Project and complies with Section §15070(a) of the
CEQA Guidelines (14 California Code of Regulations [CCR] §15000 et seq.).

This document, therefore, is a MND and incorporates all of the elements of an IS. This IS/MND has been
prepared in accordance with all criteria, standards, and procedures of CEQA (California PRC §21000 et
seq.) and the CEQA Guidelines, §15070-§15075. This is an informational document intended for use by
The City of Palmdale, Trustee and Responsible agencies, and members of the general public in
evaluating the physical environmental effects resulting from planning, constructing, and operating the
proposed Project. CEQA requires that a proposed project be reviewed to determine the environmental
effects that would result if the project is approved and implemented. The Lead Agency therefore has
the responsibility for preparing the associated environmental document prior to consideration of the
approval of the proposed project and has the authority to make decisions regarding discretionary
actions relating to implementation of the project. Appropriate mitigation measures that minimize or
avoid the proposed project impacts to the natural and built environment, are also included in the
analysis under this IS/MND.

The purpose of this IS/MND is to evaluate the potential environmental impacts of the proposed Project.
As described in the environmental checklist (Chapter 3), the Project would not result in any unmitigated
significant environmental impacts. Therefore, an IS/MND is the appropriate document for compliance
with the requirements of CEQA. This IS/MND conforms to these requirements and to the content
requirements of State CEQA Guidelines Section §15070-§15075.

This IS/MND has been prepared in accordance with the relevant provisions of CEQA (California PRC
Section §21000 et seq. Upon completion of the IS/MND, it was determined that mitigation would
reduce project environmental impacts to levels below significance thresholds; therefore, an
Environmental Impact Report would not be required and a MND would be the appropriate level of
CEQA document.

  CEQA Process
The City of Palmdale has determined that this IS and its supporting reference material provide
substantial evidence that an IS/MND is the appropriate environmental document for the proposed
project. Therefore, a good-faith effort has been made during the preparation of this IS/MND to contact
affected agencies, organizations, and persons who may have an interest in this project. In reviewing
the IS/MND, public agencies and the interested public should focus on the sufficiency of the document
in identifying and analyzing the project’s possible impacts on the environment. A Notice of Intent (NOI)
to adopt the IS/MND will be distributed for public review with the IS/MND. The NOI identifies the
location(s) where the IS/MND, the Mitigation, Monitoring and Reporting Program (MMRP), and the
associated Technical Appendices that support the IS/MND, are available for public review. Following
the public review period, the City will review any comment letters received and determine whether
any substantive comments (as defined by CEQA Guideline §15073.5(b)) were provided that may
warrant revisions to the CEQA document. If no substantial revisions are necessary, then the IS/MND
will be reviewed by the City decision-maker(s) to adopt this IS/MND. Following approval, a Notice of
Determination (NOD) for the IS/MND will be filed with the Los Angeles County Clerk.

   2  PROJECT DESCRIPTION

  Project Description
This section of the IS/MND describes the proposed Project and provides a description of the
proposed Project’s location, objectives, and required approvals. The purpose of the proposed
Project is to provide additional fuel service and commercial (gas station associated commercial
uses) within the city of Palmdale.

  Project Location
Regional Setting
The approximately six (6.09) acres site (Assessor’s Parcel Numbers [APN] 3004-016-032) is
located in the City of Palmdale, Palmdale, California. The Angeles National Forest, Mt. San
Antonio, Mt Gleason, Pacifico Mountain over five miles south of the Project site. Palmdale Lake
is located half a mile to the east of the site, while the Pacific Ocean is over 60 miles west of
the Project site. As shown on Exhibit 1 through Exhibit 4, Regional Map and Location Map,
regional access to the proposed Project site is provided by SR-14, also known as the
Antelope Valley freeway, which is less than approximately one and a fourth miles to the east
of the site, SR-138 is approximately one and a half miles north of the proposed Project site.
The Palmdale Regional Airport is approximately over five miles to the northeast. The City of
Lancaster is to the north of the Project site, and the City of Santa Clarita to the southwest of
the Project site. Cities to the east of the site are Adelanto, Victorville and Hesperia.

Surrounding Land Uses and Zoning Designations
Project located north of Avenue S and approximately 180 feet west of SR- 14, in the city of
Palmdale, County of Los Angeles. California. Land uses to the north, east, south, and west of
the east consist primarily of vacant land, hiking trail and recreational uses and some small
commercial uses in the form of a small market and a park and ride.

Current Land Use and Zoning Designations
According to the City’s General Plan Land Use Map (City of Palmdale, Land Use Map 2022) the
site area is designated as Neighborhood Commercial. According to the City’s Zoning Map, the
site is zoned Neighborhood Commercial (NC), however the applicant is requesting a change of
zone to Regional Commercial (RC). (City of Palmdale, Land Use Map 2022).

Existing Project Site
As illustrated by Exhibit 3, Project Site, the proposed Project site is currently vacant land
surrounded by vacant land to the north and west. The site is adjacent to SR-14 to the east and
Avenue S to the south.

The proposed 5,637 square-foot fueling station with a convenience store would be located on
an approximate six (6.09) acre site in the City of Palmdale.

The Project site is located within the southern portion of the Mojave Geomorphic Province,
with the San Andreas Fault Zone passing though the northeast corner of the site (City of
Palmdale General Plan Update EIR; 2022). The San Andreas Fault is an active fault and is
expected to be the source of major earthquakes within the next 30 years with a Richter
magnitude exceeding 8. The site is within a seismic hazard liquefaction zone (City of Palmdale
General Plan Update EIR; 2022).

The Project site is in the Antelope Valley Watershed of the Antelope Valley Groundwater Basin
(City of Palmdale General Plan Update EIR; 2022).

The proposed Project site is located in the Antelope Valley Air Pollution Control District. The
AVAPCD covers a portion of the Mojave Desert Air Basin, which includes the northeast portion
of Los Angeles County where the proposed Project site is located. (California Air Resources
Board; 2023).

Proposed Project Characteristics
The proposed Project would include the construction of 24 fuel pumps, air pump station, two
underground fuel storage tanks, an approximately 5,600 square foot convenience store with
operational characteristics, hours of operation are 24 hrs. seven days a week, storage
generators, on-site alternative waste water treatment system, and a covered trash enclosure
(see Exhibit 4 Conceptual Site Plan). Building heights would vary from 29 feet at the highest

Signage at the site would be limited to one free standing sign at the site’s entrance and one

ADA parking, one of which is van accessible. Access to the site would be provided along Avenue

The applicant has applied for a General Plan Amendment to allow for the use of a on-site
alternative wastewater treatment system until public sanitary sewer is available within 200 feet

Landscaping, Lighting, and Signage
The proposed Project would provide landscaped areas around the site perimeter. Landscaped
areas would consist of native trees and flowering shrubs and comply with Title 14 and 17 of the
City of Palmdale Municipal Code (PMC)

Lighting on the Project site would be provided along the eastern and southern boundaries of
the site, as well as on the exterior of the convenience store building. Standalone light poles as
well as exterior lights would be provided in the parking areas, fuel stations and fuel pump
canopy. Lighting for the Project will comply with PMC section 17.86.040.

While the proposed fuel station and convenience store would have exterior signage on the
building, a free-standing sign would be located along Avenue S between the site’s access
driveways. Signage cannot exceed 30 feet per the PMC Chapter 17.88 or exceed 100 square
feet of sign area.

Circulation
Regional and local traffic to the site is primarily provided via SR-14 which traverses the City in
a north-south direction. Avenue S, Tierra Subida Avenue, and 7th St West are designated
crosstown roadways that provide access to the site. The City’s General Plan classifies SR-14 as
a regional roadway, Avenue S as a Crosstown roadway, and the other surrounding streets as
Neighborhood roadways (City of Palmdale 2045 General Plan Update; 2022). Located to the
west of the SR-14 off-ramp and to the north of Avenue S, the proposed Project site would be
accessed through two access driveways along Avenue S. Internal site circulation would be
provided with an internal circulation system between the proposed convenience store and
restaurant as well as the fuel pumping stations. 35 parking spaces and four handicap accessible
parking areas would be provided along the convenience store of the Project site.

Ozone is a secondary pollutant as it is not directly emitted. Ozone is the result of chemical reactions
between other pollutants, most importantly hydrocarbons and NO2, which occur only in the presence of
bright sunlight. Pollutants emitted from upwind cities react during transport downwind to produce the
oxidant concentrations experienced in the area. Many areas of the AVAQMD contribute to the ozone
levels experienced at the monitoring station, with the more significant areas being those directly upwind.
Carbon Monoxide
CO is another important pollutant that is due mainly to motor vehicles. During the 2019 to 2021
monitoring period, the Federal one-hour and eight-hour concentration standards for CO were not
exceeded.
Nitrogen Dioxide
During the 2019 to 2021 monitoring period, the Federal one-hour concentration standard for Nitrogen
Dioxide has not been exceeded.

Sulfur Dioxide
The Lancaster Station did not have SO2 data available for the last three years.

Particulate Matter
During the 2019 to 2021 monitoring period, the Federal 24-hour PM10 concentration standard was
exceeded between one and two days per year at the Lancaster Station.
During the same period, the Federal 24-hour standard for PM2.5 was exceeded nine days in 2020 and one
day in 2021 the Lancaster Station.
According to the US Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA), some people are much more sensitive
than others to breathing fine particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5). People with influenza, chronic
respiratory and cardiovascular diseases, and the elderly may suffer worsening illness and premature death
due to breathing these fine particles. People with bronchitis can expect aggravated symptoms from
breathing in fine particles. Children may experience decline in lung function due to breathing in PM10 and
PM2.5. Other groups considered sensitive are smokers and people who cannot breathe well through their
noses. Exercising athletes are also considered sensitive because many breathe through their mouths
during exercise.

The Project Area’s Attainment Status
The US EPA and the California Air Resources Board (CARB) designate air basins where ambient air quality
standards are exceeded as nonattainment areas. If standards are met, the area is designated as an
attainment area. If there is inadequate or inconclusive data to make a definitive attainment designation,
they are considered unclassified. National nonattainment areas are further designated as marginal,
moderate, serious, severe, or extreme as a function of deviation from standards. Each standard has a
different definition, or form of what constitutes attainment, based on specific air quality statistics. For
example, the Federal eight-hour CO standard is not to be exceeded more than once per year; therefore,
an area is in attainment of the CO standard if no more than one eight-hour ambient air monitoring values
exceeds the threshold per year. In contrast, the federal annual PM2.5 standard is met if the three-year

Modeling Parameters and Assumptions

Construction
Typical emission rates from construction activities were obtained from CalEEMod Version 2022.1.1.20
CalEEMod is a computer model published by the SCAQMD for estimating air pollutant emissions. The
CalEEMod program uses the EMFAC2017 computer program to calculate the emission rates specific for
the Mojave Desert portion of Los Angeles County for construction-related employee vehicle trips and the
OFFROAD2011 computer program to calculate emission rates for heavy truck operations. EMFAC2017 and
OFFROAD2011 are computer programs generated by CARB that calculates composite emission rates for
vehicles. Emission rates are reported by the program in grams per trip and grams per mile or grams per
running hour. Using CalEEMod, the peak daily air pollutant emissions were calculated and presented
below. These emissions represent the highest level of emissions for each of the construction phases in
terms of air pollutant emissions.

Operational or long-term emissions will occur over the life of the Project. Both mobile and area sources

consume natural gas, gasoline-powered landscape equipment, and architectural coatings (painting).
Mobile source emissions from motor vehicles are the largest single long-term source of air pollutants from
the operation of the Project. Small amounts of emissions would also occur from area sources such as the
consumption of natural gas for heating, hearths, from landscaping emissions, and consumer product
usage. The operational emissions were estimated using the latest version of CalEEMod.

Mobile Sources
Mobile sources include emissions from the additional vehicle miles generated from the proposed Project.
The vehicle trips associated with the proposed Project are based upon the trip generation rates given in
the Traffic Scoping Agreement (Integrated Engineering Group, 2023) which uses the ITE 11th Trip
Generation Manual.

The program then applies the emission factors for each trip which is provided by the EMFAC2017 model
to determine the vehicular traffic pollutant emissions. The CalEEMod default trip lengths were used in this
analysis. Please see CalEEMod output comments sections in Appendix A for details.

Area Sources
Area sources include emissions from consumer products, landscape equipment and architectural
coatings. Landscape maintenance includes fuel combustion emissions from equipment such as lawn
mowers, rototillers, shredders/grinders, blowers, trimmers, chain saws, and hedge trimmers, as well as
air compressors, generators, and pumps. As specifics were not known about the landscaping equipment
fleet, CalEEMod defaults were used to estimate emissions from landscaping equipment.

c) Expose sensitive receptors to substantial pollutant concentrations?
  Less Than Significant Impact. The proposed Project would not exceed construction or operational
  emissions thresholds set by the AVAQMD. Impacts shall be less than significant.
  Operations-Related Human Health Impacts
  As stated previously, regarding health effects related to criteria pollutant emissions, the applicable
  significance thresholds are established for regional compliance with the state and federal ambient air
  quality standards, which are intended to protect public health from both acute and long-term health
  impacts, depending on the potential effects of the pollutant. Since regional emissions of criteria pollutants
  during operation of the proposed Project would be below the applicable thresholds, it would not
  contribute to long-term health impacts related to nonattainment of the ambient air quality standards.
  Therefore, less than significant adverse acute health impacts as a result of proposed Project operation are
  anticipated.

  CO Hot Spot Emissions
  CO is the pollutant of major concern along roadways because the most notable source of CO is motor
  vehicles. For this reason, CO concentrations are usually indicative of the local air quality generated by a
  roadway network and are used as an indicator of potential local air quality impacts. Local air quality

  impacts can be assessed by comparing future without and with proposed Project CO levels to the State
  and Federal CO standards.

  To determine if the proposed Project could cause emission levels in excess of the CO standards, a
  sensitivity analysis is typically conducted to determine the potential for CO hot spots at a number of
  intersections in the general Project vicinity. Due to reduced speeds and vehicle queuing, hot spots
  potentially can occur at high traffic volume intersections with a Level of Service (LOS) E or worse.

  Micro-scale air quality emissions have traditionally been analyzed in environmental documents where the
  air basin was a non-attainment area for CO. However, the SCAQMD has demonstrated in the CO
  attainment redesignation request to EPA that there are no hot spots anywhere in the air basin, even at
  intersections with much higher volumes, much worse congestion, and much higher background CO levels
  than anywhere in Los Angeles County. If the worst-case intersections in the air basin have no hot spot
  potential, any local impacts will be below thresholds.

  Traffic analysis from Integrated Engineering Group (2023) showed that the proposed Project would
  generate 1,543 average daily trips. The 1992 Federal Attainment Plan for Carbon Monoxide (1992 CO Plan)
  showed that an intersection which has a daily traffic volume of approximately 100,000 vehicles per day
  would not violate the CO standard. The volume of traffic at Project buildout would be well below 100,000
  vehicles and below the necessary volume to even get close to causing a violation of the CO standard.
  Therefore, no CO hot spot modeling was performed and less than significant long-term air quality impact
  is anticipated to local air quality with the on-going use of the proposed Project.

  Cumulative Regional Air Quality Impacts
  Cumulative Projects include local development as well as general growth within the proposed Project
  area. However, as with most development, the greatest source of emissions is from mobile sources, which
  travel well out of the local area. Therefore, from an air quality standpoint, the cumulative analysis would
  extend beyond any local Projects and when wind patterns are considered, would cover an even larger
  area. Accordingly, the cumulative analysis for the proposed Project’s air quality must be generic by
  nature.

  The proposed Project area is out of attainment for both ozone and PM10 particulate matter. Construction
  and operation of cumulative Projects will further degrade the local air quality, as well as the air quality of
  the Mojave Desert Air Basin. The greatest cumulative impact on the quality of regional air cell will be the
  incremental addition of pollutants mainly from increased traffic from residential, commercial, and
  industrial development and the use of heavy equipment and trucks associated with the construction of
  these Projects. Air quality will be temporarily degraded during construction activities that occur separately
  or simultaneously. However, in accordance with the AVAQMD methodology, Projects that do not exceed
  the AVAQMD criteria or can be mitigated to less than criteria levels are not significant and do not add to
  the overall cumulative impact. The proposed Project does not exceed any of the thresholds of significance
  and therefore is considered less than significant.

For purposes of CEQA, a historic resource is any object, building, structure, site, area, place, record, or
manuscript listed in or eligible for listing in the California Register of Historical Resources (CRHR) (PRC
§5024.1, Title 14 CCR, §4852). A resource is eligible for listing in the CRHR if it meets any of the following
criteria:

  •  Is associated with events that have made a significant contribution to the broad patterns of
  California’s history and cultural heritage.
  •  Is associated with the lives of persons important in our past.
  •  Embodies the distinctive characteristics of a type, period, region, or method of construction, or
  represents the work of an important creative individual, or possesses high artistic values.
  •  Has yielded, or may be likely to yield, information important to prehistory or history.

Prehistoric archaeological sites are typically evaluated only under Criterion 4 for their potential to yield
data important to understanding the prehistory of the area or region. Historical archaeological sites and
architectural resources may be evaluated under any of the four criteria because their features, plus
available historical documentation, may be used to inform our understanding of their association with

Less Than Significant Impact. The potential severity of ground shaking during an earthquake depends on
a variety of factors and location of seismic zones. Seismic zones are used to describe an area where
earthquakes tend to focus. The proposed Project site is within Seismic Zone 4, meaning that there is a one
in 10 chance that an earthquake with an active peak acceleration level of 0.4g will occur within 50 years.
The proposed Project would include the construction of 24 fuel pumps and air pump station, two
underground fuel storage tanks, an approximately 5,600 square foot convenience store with an outdoor
patio space, a generator, and a covered trash enclosure. The proposed Project would also include 39
parking spaces, two of the 39 spaces are designated ADA parking, one of which is van accessible. Avenue
S, Tierra Subida Avenue, and 7th St West are designated crosstown roadways that provide access to the
site.

A Geotechnical Engineering Study was completed by CMT Technical Services in September 2022 for the
proposed Project site (Appendix D). Both the Geotechnical Study as well as the City of Palmdale 2045
General Plan Update EIR (City of Palmdale; 2022) identify the proposed Project site in the San Andreas
Fault zone, which bisects the northwest corner of the site (Figure 4.7-3). The San Andreas Fault is expected
to be the source of major earthquakes within the next 30 years with a Richter magnitude exceeding 8.0.
Therefore, seismic ground shaking and surface ruptures, in the event of an earthquake, could be
experienced on the proposed Project site due to seismic activity along the San Andreas Fault. The
proposed Project would therefore be required to be designed and constructed in accordance with State
and City of Palmdale building codes to reduce the potential for exposure of people or structures to seismic
risks to the maximum extent possible. The proposed Project would also be required to comply with the
seismic safety requirements in the latest California Building Code (CBC) as well as the PMC. Compliance
with such requirements would reduce seismic ground shaking and surface rupture impacts to a less than
significant level.
The Geotechnical study also included design recommendations for the proposed Project:
Foundation Recommendations
  • Footings may be designed using a net bearing pressure of 2,000 psf if bearing on scarified and re-
  compacted natural soils, and 2,500 psf if bearing on a minimum of 18 inches of structural fill
  placed upon scarified, re-compacted natural soils.
  • Exterior footings subject to frost should be placed at least 18 inches below final grade, or per city
  standards if deeper.
  • Interior footings not subject to frost should be placed at least 12 inches below grade.
  • Continuous footing widths should be maintained at a minimum of 18 inches.
  • Spot footings should be a minimum of 24 inches wide.
Installation
  • foundations shall not be placed on undocumented fill, topsoil with organics, sod, rubbish,
  construction debris, other deleterious materials, frozen soils, or within ponded water.
  • The minimum thickness of structural fill below footings should be equivalent to one-third the
  thickness of structural fill below any other portion of the foundations.

  No Impact. Liquefaction typically occurs when saturated, loose sandy soils lose their support capabilities
  due to pressure from a seismic event. Even clayey soils, if saturated, will generally not liquefy during a
  major seismic event. The Geotechnical Engineering Study by CMT Technical Services in September 2022
  (Appendix D) undertaken for the proposed Project site, accounted for mainly slightly moist Sandy SILT
  (ML), Sandy SILTY CLAY (CL-ML) sand, slightly moist Silty SAND (SM) and some loose gravel. Although the
  City of Palmdale 2045 General Plan Update EIR (City of Palmdale; 2022) shows the site to be located within
  a liquefaction zone (Figure 4.7-5), the Geotechnical Engineering Study (Appendix D) does not report the
  presence of groundwater that would affect the sandy soils on the site. Therefore, there would be no
  impact from liquefaction.

underground fuel storage tanks, an approximately 5,600 square foot convenience store with an outdoor
patio space, a generator, and a covered trash enclosure. The proposed Project would also include 39
parking spaces, two of the 39 spaces are designated ADA parking, one of which is van accessible. Avenue

An Air Quality, Greenhouse Gas, Energy Impact Study was conducted by MD Acoustics LLC in November
2023 (Appendix A). Constituent gases of the Earth’s atmosphere, called atmospheric greenhouse gases
(GHG), play a critical role in the Earth’s radiation amount by trapping infrared radiation emitted from the
Earth’s surface, which otherwise would have escaped to space. Prominent greenhouse gases contributing
to this process include carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), ozone, water vapor, nitrous oxide (N2O),
and chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs). This phenomenon, known as the Greenhouse Effect, is responsible for
maintaining a habitable climate. Anthropogenic (caused or produced by humans) emissions of these
greenhouse gases in excess of natural ambient concentrations are responsible for the enhancement of
the Greenhouse Effect and have led to a trend of unnatural warming of the Earth’s natural climate, known
as global warming or climate change. Emissions of gases that induce global warming are attributable to
human activities associated with industrial/manufacturing, agricultural, utilities, transportation, and
residential land uses. Transportation is responsible for 41 percent of the State’s greenhouse gas
emissions, followed by electricity generation. Emissions of CO2 and nitrous oxide (NO2) are byproducts
of fossil fuel combustion. Methane, a potent greenhouse gas, results from off-gassing associated with
agricultural practices and landfills. Sinks of CO2, where CO2 is stored outside of the atmosphere, include
uptake by vegetation and dissolution into the ocean. Table 16 Description of Greenhouse Gases provides
a description of each of the greenhouse gases and their global warming potential.

California Air Resources Board (CARB) Scoping Plan Consistency
The CARB approved a Climate Change Scoping Plan in December 2008. The Scoping Plan outlines the
State’s strategy to achieve the 2020 greenhouse gas emissions limit. The Scoping Plan proposes a
comprehensive set of actions designed to reduce overall greenhouse gas emissions in California, improve
our environment, reduce our dependence on oil, diversify our energy sources, save energy, create new
jobs, and enhance public health (California Air Resources Board 2008). The measures in the Scoping Plan
have been in place since 2012.

This Scoping Plan calls for an ambitious but achievable reduction in California’s greenhouse gas emissions,
cutting approximately 30 percent from business-as-usual emission levels projected for 2020, or about 10
percent from today’s levels. On a per-capita basis, that means reducing annual emissions of 14 tons of
carbon dioxide for every man, woman and child in California down to about 10 tons per person by 2020.

In May 2014, CARB released its First Update to the Climate Change Scoping Plan (CARB 2014). This Update
identifies the next steps for California’s leadership on climate change. While California continues on its
path to meet the near-term 2020 greenhouse gas limit, it must also set a clear path toward long-term,
deep GHG emission reductions. This report highlights California’s success to date in reducing its GHG

State’s climate goals, and includes a description of a suite of specific actions to meet the State’s 2030 GHG
limit. In addition, Chapter 4 provides a broader description of the many actions and proposals being

Guided by legislative direction, the actions identified in the 2017 Scoping Plan reduce overall GHG

low carbon economy. The 2017 Scoping Plan builds upon the successful framework established by the
Initial Scoping Plan and First Update, while identifying new, technologically feasible, and cost-effective
strategies to ensure that California meets its GHG reduction targets in a way that promotes and rewards
innovation, continues to foster economic growth, and delivers improvements to the environment and
public health, including in disadvantaged communities. The Plan includes policies to require direct GHG
reductions at some of the State’s largest stationary sources and mobile sources. These policies include
the use of lower GHG fuels, efficiency regulations, and the Cap-and Trade Program, which constrains and
reduces emissions at covered sources.

An Environmental Site Assessment (ESA) was conducted on August 22, 2022. The study concluded that
there were no site concerns, there were no hazardous substances or petroleum products observed on the
subject property during the site assessment. Hazardous materials regulations, which are codified in Titles
8, 22, 26, and 49 of the California Code of Regulations (CCR) as well as in the California Health and Safety

human health and the environment from the routine use of hazardous substances. Protection against

surface areas; oil/water separators or physical barriers in catch basins or storm drains; vapor emissions

Code Section, which requires that hazardous materials be transported using designated routes and with
the lowest travel time between destinations.

as they are considered hazardous if not stored or handled properly. Additionally, typical building
construction materials like paints, adhesives, solvents, and similar substances will be present at the
construction site. Mishandling, improper storage, or transportation of these hazardous materials can lead
to accidental releases or spills, potentially endangering the health of workers, the public, and the

Fundamentals of Noise

Sound, Noise and Acoustics
Sound is a disturbance created by a moving or vibrating source and is capable of being detected by the
hearing organs. Sound may be thought of as mechanical energy of a moving object transmitted by
pressure waves through a medium to a human ear. For traffic or stationary noise, the medium of concern
is air. Noise is defined as sound that is loud, unpleasant, unexpected, or unwanted.

Frequency and Hertz
A continuous sound is described by its frequency (pitch) and its amplitude (loudness). Frequency relates
to the number of pressure oscillations per second. Low-frequency sounds are low in pitch (bass sounding)
and high-frequency sounds are high in pitch (squeak). These oscillations per second (cycles) are commonly
referred to as Hertz (Hz). The human ear can hear from the bass pitch starting at 20 Hz to the high pitch
of 20,000 Hz.

Sound Pressure Levels and Decibels
The amplitude of a sound determines its loudness. The loudness of sound increases or decreases as the
amplitude increases or decreases. Sound pressure amplitude is measured in units of micro-Newton per
square inch meter (N/m2), also called micro-Pascal (µPa). One µPa is approximately one hundred
billionths (0.00000000001) of normal atmospheric pressure. Sound pressure level (SPL or Lp) is used to
describe in logarithmic units the ratio of actual sound pressures to a reference pressure squared. These
units are called decibels abbreviated dB. Table 20 Typical A-Weighted Noise Levels below illustrates
references sound levels for different noise sources.

  Table 20  Typical A-Weighted Noise Levels

Since decibels are typically on a logarithmic scale, sound pressure levels cannot be added or subtracted
by simple plus or minus addition. When two sounds or equal SPL are combined, they will produce an SPL
three dB greater than the original single SPL. In other words, sound energy must be doubled to produce a
three dB increase. If two sounds differ by approximately 10 dB, the higher sound level is the predominant
sound.

Human Response to Changes in Noise Levels
In general, the healthy human ear is most sensitive to sounds between 1,000 Hz and 5,000 Hz, (A-weighted
scale) and it perceives a sound within that range as being more intense than a sound with a higher or
lower frequency with the same magnitude. For purposes of this report as well as with most environmental
documents, the A-scale weighting is typically reported in terms of A-weighted decibel (dBA). Typically, the
human ear can barely perceive a change in the noise level of three dB. A change in five dB is readily
perceptible, and a change in 10 dB is perceived as being twice or half as loud. As previously discussed, a
doubling of sound energy results in a three dB increase in sound, which means that a doubling of sound
energy (e.g., doubling the volume of traffic on a highway) would result in a barely perceptible change in
sound level.

Noise Descriptors
Noise in our daily environment fluctuates over time. Some noise levels occur in regular patterns, others
are random. Some noise levels are constant while others are sporadic. Noise descriptors were created to
describe the different time-varying noise levels.

A-Weighted Sound Level: The sound pressure level in decibels as measured on a sound level meter using
the A-weighted filter network. The A-weighting filter de-emphasizes the very low and very high-frequency
components of the sound in a manner similar to the response of the human ear. A numerical method of
rating human judgment of loudness.

Ambient Noise Level: The composite of noise from all sources, near and far. In this context, the ambient
noise level constitutes the normal or existing level of environmental noise at a given location.

Community Noise Equivalent Level (CNEL): The average equivalent A-weighted sound level during a 24-
hour day, obtained after the addition of five decibels to sound levels in the evening from 7:00 PM to 10:00
PM and after the addition of 10 decibels to sound levels in the night before 7:00 AM and after 10:00 PM.

Decibel (dB): A unit for measuring the amplitude of a sound, equal to 20 times the logarithm to the base
10 of the ratio of the pressure of the sound measured to the reference pressure, which is 20 micro-pascals.

dB(A): A-weighted sound level (see definition above).

Equivalent Sound Level (LEQ): The sound level corresponding to a steady noise level over a given sample
period with the same amount of acoustic energy as the actual time-varying noise level. The energy
average noise level during the sample period.

Habitable Room: Any room meeting the requirements of the Uniform Building Code, or other applicable
regulations, which is intended to be used for sleeping, living, cooking, or dining purposes, excluding such
enclosed spaces as closets, pantries, bath or toilet rooms, service rooms, connecting corridors, laundries,
unfinished attics, foyers, storage spaces, cellars, utility rooms, and similar spaces.

L(n): The A-weighted sound level exceeded during a certain percentage of the sample time. For example,
L10 in the sound level exceeded 10 percent of the sample time. Similarly, L50, L90, and L99, etc.

Traffic Noise Prediction
Noise levels associated with traffic depends on a variety of factors: (1) volume of traffic, (2) speed of
traffic, (3) auto, medium truck (2 axle), and heavy truck percentage (three axle and greater), and (4) sound
propagation. The greater the volume of traffic, the higher speeds and truck percentages equate to a
louder volume in noise. A doubling of the Average Daily Traffic (ADT) along a roadway will increase noise
levels by approximately three dB; reasons for this are discussed in the sections above.

Sound Propagation
As sound propagates from a source it spreads geometrically. Sound from a small, localized source (i.e., a
point source) radiates uniformly outward as it travels away from the source in a spherical pattern. The
sound level attenuates at a rate of six dB per doubling of distance. The movement of vehicles down a
roadway makes the source of the sound appear to propagate from a line (i.e., line source) rather than a
point source. This line source results in the noise propagating from a roadway in a cylindrical spreading
versus a spherical spreading that results from a point source. The sound level attenuates for a line source
at a rate of three dB per doubling of distance.

As noise propagates from the source, it is affected by the ground and atmosphere. Noise models use hard
site (reflective surfaces) and soft site (absorptive surfaces) to help calculate predicted noise levels. Hard
site conditions assume no excessive ground absorption between the noise source and the receiver. Soft
site conditions such as grass, soft dirt or landscaping attenuate noise at a rate of 1.5 dB per doubling of
distance. When added to the geometric spreading, the excess ground attenuation results in an overall
noise attenuation of 4.5 dB per doubling of distance for a line source and 7.5 dB per doubling of distance
for a point source.

Research has demonstrated that atmospheric conditions can have a significant effect on noise levels when
noise receivers are located 200 feet from a noise source. Wind, temperature, air humidity, and turbulence
can further impact how far sound can travel.

Ground-Borne Vibration Fundamentals

Vibration Descriptors
Ground-borne vibrations consist of rapidly fluctuating motions within the ground that have an average
motion of zero. The effects of ground-borne vibrations typically only cause a nuisance to people, but at
extreme vibration levels, damage to buildings may occur. Although ground-borne vibration can be felt
outdoors, it is typically only an annoyance to people indoors where the associated effects of the shaking
of a building can be notable. Ground-borne noise is an effect of ground-borne vibration and only exists
indoors since it is produced from noise radiated from the motion of the walls and floors of a room and
may also consist of the rattling of windows or dishes on shelves.

Several different methods are used to quantify vibration amplitude.

PPV – Known as the peak particle velocity (PPV) which is the maximum instantaneous peak in vibration
velocity, typically given in inches per second.

RMS – Known as root mean squared (RMS) can be used to denote vibration amplitude

VdB – A commonly used abbreviation to describe the vibration level (VdB) for a vibration source.

Vibration Perception
Typically, developed areas are continuously affected by vibration velocities of 50 VdB or lower. These
continuous vibrations are not noticeable to humans whose threshold of perception is around 65 VdB.
Outdoor sources that may produce perceptible vibrations are usually caused by construction equipment,
steel-wheeled trains, and traffic on rough roads, while smooth roads rarely produce perceptible ground-
borne noise or vibration. To counter the effects of ground-borne vibration, the Federal Transit
Administration (FTA) has published guidance relative to vibration impacts. According to the FTA, fragile
buildings can be exposed to ground-borne vibration levels of 0.3 inches per second without experiencing
structural damage.

Vibration Perception
There are three main types of vibration propagation: surface, compression, and shear waves. Surface
waves, or Rayleigh waves, travel along the ground’s surface. These waves carry most of their energy along

  analogous to airborne sound waves. S-waves, or shear waves, are also body waves that carry energy along

  As vibration waves propagate from a source, the vibration energy decreases in a logarithmic nature and

ANALYSIS METHODOLGY
The Guidelines adopted by Los Angeles County require a 4-step process for implementing SB 743 and VMT
analysis:
  •  Baseline VMT – Describes the process for determining the County Baseline VMT and describes the
  analysis methodology and VMT metrics for Los Angeles County.
  •  VMT Screening – Provides the options for project screening to determine if a VMT analysis is
  required and summarizes the VMT analysis process for projects that do not meet the screening
  criteria.
  •  VMT Impact Thresholds – Based on the required VMT Measure the Project will need to identify
  the appropriate VMT Measure threshold as required in the Guidelines.
  •  VMT Mitigation Strategies – If the Project would have a VMT impact under CEQA the Project
  would need to mitigate the impact to the extent feasible and disclose whether the Project would
  fully mitigate its impact or require additional analysis to reduce VMT and meet the County’s
  thresholds are provided.
Los Angeles County Transportation Analysis Guidelines Screening Criteria
The Guidelines recognize that certain projects based on type, location, size and other contexts could lead
to a presumption of less than significance (i.e. the project’s VMT would not cause a transportation impact)
and would not need additional VMT analysis. The Guidelines provide the following screening criteria:
  1. Project Size: A project that generates 110 or fewer daily trips.
  2. Locally Serving Retail: A project that has locally serving retail uses that are 50,000 square feet or
  less, including specialty retail, shopping center, grocery store, pharmacy, financial services/banks,
  fitness center or health club, restaurant, and café. If the project contains other land uses, those
  uses need to be considered under other applicable screening criteria.
  3. Transit Proximity: A project that is located within a half mile of a major transit stop or within a ½
  mile of a bus stop on a high-quality transit corridor (HQTC). A major transit stop is a rail station or
  a stop with two or more intersecting bus routes with service frequency of 15 minutes or less
  during commute periods. A HQTC is a corridor with fixed route bus service with frequency of 15
  minutes or less during peak commute periods. In addition, the project should have the following
  characteristics:
  o A floor Area Ratio (FAR) of 0.75 or greater
  o Is consistent with the applicable SCAG Sustainable Communities Strategy (as determined
  by the County)
  o Does not provide more parking than required by the County
  o Does not replacing affordable housing units
  4. Affordable Housing: A residential project that provides affordable housing units.
  5. Transportation Facilities: Transportation projects that promote non-auto travel, improve safety,
  or improve traffic operations at current bottlenecks, such as transit, bicycle and pedestrian
