1990). While the Project site does not contain suitable nesting habitat for this species, the site may be used
for foraging. A CNDDB occurrence of this species has been recorded approximately 2 miles northeast of the
Project site.

Costa’s Hummingbird (Calypte costae)
Costa’s hummingbird is a USFWS bird of conservation concern (BCC) with a moderate potential to occur on
the Project site. This species occurs in desert wash, edges of desert riparian and valley foothill riparian,
coastal scrub, desert succulent scrub, lower-elevation chaparral, and palm oasis. Nesting occurs in a variety of
trees, cacti, shrubs, woody forbs, and vines (Green et al. 1990). The Project site contains suitable nesting
habitat for this species.

Ferruginous Hawk (Buteo regalis)
Ferruginous hawk is a CDFW Watch List species with a moderate potential to occur on the Project site. This
species occurs in open grasslands, sagebrush flats, low foothills, surrounding valleys, and fringes of pinyon-
juniper habitats. Prey primarily consists of lagomorphs, ground squirrels, and mice (Polite et al. 1999) . Due
to the abundance of suitable prey species present on the Project site, this species may use the Project site for
feeding. A CNDDB occurrence of this species has been recorded approximately four miles northwest of the
Project site.

LeConte’s Thrasher (Toxostoma lecontei)
LeConte’s thrasher is a USFWS BCC and a CDFW SSC with a high potential to occur on the Project site. This
species occurs in open desert wash, desert scrub, alkali desert scrub, Joshua tree woodland, and desert
succulent habitats. Scattered desert shrubs and cactus are relied of for cover and nesting occurs in dense,
spiny shrubs or densely branched cactus in desert wash habitat (Dobkin et al. 2005). The Project site contains
suitable vegetation for this species. Two CNDDB occurences of this species have been recorded within 5 miles
of the Project site.

Loggerhead Shrike (Lanius ludovicianus)
Loggerhead shrike is a CDFW SSC with a high potential to occur on the Project site. This species occurs in
open-canopied valley foothill hardwood, valley foothill hardwood-conifer, valley foothill riparian, pinyon-
juniper, juniper, desert riparian, and Joshua tree habitats. This species feeds on insects, small birds,
mammals, amphibians, reptiles, fish, carrion, and various other invertebrates. The Project site contains
suitable vegetation for this species (Granholm et al. 1990). A CNDDB occurrence of this species has been
recorded approximately two miles southwest of the Project site.

Swainson’s Hawk (Buteo Swainsoni)
Swainson’s hawk is a state threatened species with a high potential to occur on the Project site. This species
nests in juniper-sage flats, riparian areas, and oak savanna. This species is also found in open desert,
grassland, and cropland. Their diet consists of mice, gophers, ground squirrels, rabbits, large arthropods,
amphibians, reptiles and birds. Suitable nesting habitat and prey species are present on the Project site

of the Project site.

Mohave Ground Squirrel (Xerospermphilus mohavensis)
Mohave ground squirrel is a state threatened species with a high potential to occur on the Project site. This
species occurs in desert scrub, alkali desert scrub, Joshua tree woodland, and annual grasslands within the
Mohave Desert in San Bernardino, Los Angeles, Kern, and Inyo counties. This species relies on burrows at the

support this species were observed during the biological field survey. Multiple CNDDB occurences of this
species have been recorded within five miles of the Project site.

Crotch’s Bumblebee (Bombus crotchii)
Crotch’s bumblebee is a state candidate species with a high potential to occur on the Project site. This species
occurs in open grasslands, shrublands, chaparral, desert margins, Joshua tree woodland, creosote scrub, and
semi-urban settings (NaturveServe 2023a). Suitable vegetation is present on the Project site and a CNDDB
occurrence of this species has been recorded approximately 0.75-mile northeast of the Project site.

7  Discussion and Recommended Mitigation
7.1 Special-status Plants
Native Desert Vegetation Preservation
The City of Palmdale requires that a desert vegetation preservation plan be prepared and submitted as part
of the development application in order to maximize the amount of native desert vegetation that can be
preserved throughout development. The removal of native desert vegetation without the submittal of a
desert vegetation preservation plan would be considered a significant impact. As such, the following
mitigation measure is recommended to reduce impacts to less than significant:

  •  A written report and site plan which depicts the location of each California juniper, discusses their
  age and health, and identifies and locates all trees and shrubs which can be saved in place or located.

  •  A site landscaping plan showing the proposed locations of all Joshua trees, California junipers, and
  any other native desert vegetation that will remain on-site.
  •  A long-term maintenance program for any desert vegetation preserved on the site. The minimum term
  of any maintenance program shall be two growing seasons, unless a shorter length of time is
  determined by the City’s Landscape Architect, or in lieu thereof, the Director of Public Works’
  designee, in cases where the trees retained on the site are of such health and vigor after one growing

  •  Such other and further information as the Director of Planning may deem necessary to fulfill the

 Additionally, a minimum standard of preservation for California juniper shall be met by the Project developer
in accordance with Section 14.04.070 of the City of Palmdale municipal code. If this standard cannot be met,
the developer shall pay all associated in-lieu fees as required by the City.

Short-Joint Beavertail
If present on the Project site, the removal of native desert vegetation would result in the removal of short-
joint beavertail, which would be considered a significant impact. As such, the following mitigation measure is
recommended to reduce Project impacts to less than significant:

Prior to the commencement of construction activities, a floristic survey shall be conducted for short-joint
beavertail. If detected, each individual shall be flagged or fenced for avoidance prior to the commencement
of construction activities. If avoidance is not feasible, a qualified biologist shall develop a short-join beavertail
removal and reintroduction plan for any impacted plants. This plan must be approved by CDFW prior to the
issuance of grading permits.

Western Joshua Tree
The Project site contains a total of 120 individual western Joshua trees. The Project would require the
removal of some, if not all, of these trees, which would be considered a significant impact. As such, the
following mitigation measure is recommended to reduce Project impacts to less than significant:

Impacts to western Joshua trees shall be avoided to the extent feasible. A buffer shall be placed around each
Western Joshua tree that can be preserved at a minimum distance of five feet beyond the tree’s drip line.
Temporary fencing, signage, and flagging shall be erected to prevent impacts to the tree and buffered area
for the duration of construction activities.

In the event that western Joshua trees cannot be preserved during Project construction or operation, an
Incidental Take Permit for the removal of western Joshua trees shall be obtained from CDFW prior to the
removal of western Joshua trees and the issuance of any grading or construction permit. In addition, all
applicable fees as established in the Western Joshua Tree Conservation Act shall be paid by the Project
developer prior to the removal of any western Joshua trees.

7.2 Special-status Wildlife
California Glossy Snake, Coast Horned Lizard, and Northern California Legless Lizard
Construction activities on the Project site may result in direct impacts to California glossy snake, coast horned
lizard, and Northern California legless lizard. As such, the following mitigation measure is recommended to
reduce Project impacts to less than significant:

No more than 72 hours prior to the commencement of construction activities, a qualified biologist shall
conduct a survey for California glossy snake, coast horned lizard, and Northern California legless lizard. If any
of these species are found to be present on the Project site, no construction activities shall commence until
the individuals have left the area or have been relocated by a qualified biologist in accordance with CDFW
protocols.

Desert Tortoise
Grading and vegetation removal activities may result in direct impacts to desert tortoise. As such, the
following mitigation measure is recommended to reduce Project impacts to less than significant:

Prior to the commencement of construction activities, a qualified biologist shall conduct clearance surveys
for desert tortoise on the Project site. Clearance surveys shall follow the USFWS Clearance Survey Protocol for
the Mojave Desert Tortoise (May 2019). If desert tortoise is determined to be present on the Project site, the
Project developer shall develop and implement a mitigation and monitoring plan in consultation with USFWS
and CDFW.

Burrowing Owl
Grading and vegetation removal activities on the Project site may result in direct impacts to burrowing owl,
which would be considered a significant impact. As such, the following mitigation measure is recommended to
reduce Project impacts to less than significant:

No more than 30 days prior to the commencement of construction activities, a qualified biologist shall survey
the Project site to determine whether burrowing owl occur on the site. If burrowing owl is found to be present
on the Project site, CDFW shall be consulted, and all applicable protocols, as established by CDFW, shall be
adhered to prior the commencement of construction activities.

Nesting Birds
The removal of vegetation during the nesting bird season may result in direct impacts to nesting birds, which
would be considered a significant impact. As such, the following mitigation measure is recommended to reduce
Project impacts to less than significant:

To the extent feasible, construction-related activities shall be conducted outside of the nesting bird season
(February 1 through August 31). If construction must occur during the nesting bird season, a qualified biologist
shall conduct a nesting bird survey of the Project site no more than 72 hours prior to the commencement of
vegetation removal activities. If no active nests or breeding activities are found, construction activities may

shall be delineated by a biological monitor, and a buffer of no less than 300 feet (500 feet for raptors) shall be
established in which no construction activities are permitted until the nest becomes inactive, the young have

longer be impacted by the Project.

Mohave Ground Squirrel
Grading and vegetation removal activities on the Project site may result in direct impacts to Mohave ground
squirrel, which would be considered a significant impact. As such, the following mitigation measure is
recommended to reduce Project impacts to less than significant:

Prior to the commencement of construction activities, a qualified biologist shall conduct surveys for Mohave
ground squirrel in accordance with the California Department of Fish and Game Mohave Ground Squirrel Survey
Guidelines (January 2003). Surveys for Mohave ground squirrel are performed between March 15 and July 15
using standard live trapping techniques. A total of three rounds of trapping are required during this time,
although trapping shall cease once a Mohave ground squirrel is captured or observed. If these surveys obtain
positive results for Mohave ground squirrel, or if Mohave ground squirrel presence is assumed within the
Project site, the Project developer shall obtain incidental take authorization from CDFW prior to the
commencement of construction activities.

Crotch’s Bumblebee
Construction activities may result in direct impacts to crotch’s bumblebee, which would be considered a
significant impact. As such, the following mitigation measure is recommended to reduce Project impacts to
less than significant:

Prior to the commencement of construction activities, a qualified biologist shall conduct a survey for Crotch’s
bumblebee during the species’ active period (March to July). This survey shall include a search for Crotch’s
bumblebee activity and the presence of ground nests. If a ground nest is observed, the nest shall remain in
place until it is determined to be no longer active by a qualified biologist. If Crotch’s bumblebee is present on
the Project site and may occur during Project activities, the Project developer shall consult with CDFW
regarding the implementation of avoidance measures, or the issuance of an Incidental Take Permit.

be considered a significant impact. As such, the following mitigation measure is recommended to reduce
Project impacts to less than significant:

CULTURAL AND ENVIRONMENTAL SETTING

Environmental Setting

The project area is located on the western edge of southern California’s Antelope Valley and
within the southwestern Mojave Desert. The Antelope Valley is approximately 3,000 square
miles. On the northwest, it is separated from the San Joaquin Valley by the Tehachapi
Mountains; on the south and southwest, it is separated by the San Gabriel Mountains; and the
north and east boundaries of the Antelope Valley are distinguished by isolated buttes. The City
of Palmdale is 104 square miles and is located in the southern region of the Antelope Valley just
60 miles from downtown Los Angeles off the Antelope Valley Freeway (State Highway 14).
Angeles National Forest is south of the city, and Edwards Air Force Base is northeast. The
Project parcel is currently vacant land surrounded by other vacant parcels, with some
development on the south side of W. Avenue S across from the Project parcel.

Several vegetation types are recognized in the Mojave Zone: creosote bush scrub, saltbush scrub,
shadscale scrub, blackbrush scrub, juniper woodland, Joshua tree woodland, and annual
vegetation (Vasek and Barbour 1990). The predominant vegetative resource found in the Project
area was juniper and Joshua tree (Yucca brevifolia) woodland. Wildlife common to this area
include kangaroo rats (Dipodomys spp.), woodrats (Neotoma spp.), and various ground squirrels
(Spermophilus spp.). Larger mammals include cottontail rabbits (Sylvilagus audobonii) and
coyote (Canis latrans). The mule deer (Odocoileus hemionus) is another major resident of the
region, although its numbers have declined in modern times (Sutton 1990:67). Large numbers of
pronghom (Antilocapra americana) are presumed to have existed in the region at one time, as
well as bighorn sheep (Ovis canadensis) and black bear (Ursus americanus). Avian species
identified in the area include Northern mockingbird (Mimus polyglottus), California quail
(Cattipepla cailfornica), Common raven (Corvus corax), horned lark (Eremophila atpestris),
Great-tailed grackle (Quiscalus mexicanus), Brewer’s blackbird (Euphagus cyanocephalus),
European starling (Sturnus vulgaris), and rock dove (Columba livis).

Prehistoric Cultural Setting

Earle et al. (1997) and Loechl et al. (2002) have divided the prehistoric cultural chronology for
the Antelope Valley into seven cultural/temporal periods: Fluted Point Period, Lake Mojave
Period, Pinto Period, Gypsum Period, Saratoga Springs Period, Post-Saratoga Springs/Late
Period, and Contact/Ethnographic Period; the last includes the Euroamerican historic record.

Fluted Point Period (12,000-10,000 B.P.)
Sites dating to this period have been identified based on the presence of fluted-base projectile
points similar to the well-known Clovis forms associated with ancient cultures of the Great
Plains. Termed “Western Clovis” (Tuohy 1974; Willig and Aikens 1988), “Black Rock Concave
Base” (Clewlow 1968) or “Great Basin Concave-Base” (Pendleton 1979), many types of Clovis-
like points have been found in various locations throughout the western Great Basin and in
California. Lithic assemblages that contain fluted points often contain crescents, gravers,
scrapers, choppers, and “perforators” (Davis 1978). Fluted point sites occur in a variety of

Anna Choudhari
Page 3 of 20

environments, indicating that inhabitants were likely generalized foragers rather than big game
hunters (Earle et al. 1997; Moratto 1984).

Lake Mohave Period (10,000-7000 B.P.)
In the western Great Basin, various stemmed projectile point forms have been dated to the early
Holocene, roughly between 10,000 and 7500 B.P. Generally subsumed under the broader
appellate “Great Basin Stemmed,” these artifacts are elongate, lanceolate forms often with
subtle, sloping shoulders, but many different regional styles exist. In the western Mojave, typical
stemmed points are Lake Mohave (unshouldered) and Silver Lake forms (slightly shouldered),
both of which are parts of lithic assemblages similar to those of the Fluted Point period.

Pinto Period (7000-4000 B.P.)
Pinto points, projectiles that bear “weak” shoulders and indented or split-stem bases, typify
archaeological assemblages of this period. Associated flaked stone assemblages include leaf-
shaped bifaces, formal unifaces, flake tools, and consistent quantities of core-cobble implements
(Basgall 1993, 2000; Campbell and Campbell 1935; Hunt 1960; Rogers 1939). Lithic selection
favored fine-grained igneous stones such as basalt and rhyolite for points and bifaces.
Millingstones are a major part of Pinto period assemblages, reflecting the importance of seed
processing. The timing of the Pinto period coincides with Antevs’ (1953) Altithermal, an
extended interval when climate was supposedly very hot and dry. Archaeologists once believed a
scarcity of Pinto sites in the Mojave Desert signaled a near-total abandonment of the region
because of the oppressive climate, but recent studies imply that the middle Holocene in the
Antelope Valley was punctuated by wetter episodes (Grayson 1993; Mehringer 1986) and that
the effects of the Altithermal were variable in different parts of the desert.

Gypsum Period (4000-1500 B.P.)
Diagnostic artifacts at Gypsum period sites include Gypsum contracting-stem projectile points,
Elko Eared and Corner-notched points, and Humboldt Basal-notched points. Lithic assemblages
feature bifaces, scrapers, and a variety of other flake-based tools but also contain mortars and
pestles as evidence of processing mesquite, pine nuts, yucca, and agave. Large villages or village
complexes appear during Gypsum times, reflecting a transition from seasonal transhumance to
year-round sedentary habitation within the Antelope Valley (Sutton 1988). The presence of
marine shell artifacts at Gypsum period sites in the Antelope Valley indicates economic ties
between the Antelope Valley and the California coast (Warren 1984).

Saratoga Springs Period (1500-800 B.P.)
At around 1500 B.P., the aboriginal people of the Mojave Desert had replaced the atlatl, or spear-
thrower, with the bow and arrow. This change brought about a shift toward the use of smaller
projectile points, including various corner-notched and side-notched Saratoga Springs types and
the corner-notched Rose Spring and Eastgate types. Anasazi ceramics also appear in the southern
Mojave around 1200-1100 B.P., coinciding with the westward spread of the Virgin Anasazi into
southern Nevada. Influence from the cultures of the Colorado River brought in buff ware
ceramics and other goods. The intensification of plant use initiated during the Gypsum period
continued in the Saratoga Springs period, and diet was expanded to include a wide range of high
cost/low return plant foods that required high cost/high return procurement and processing
strategies.

Post-Saratoga Springs or Late Period (800-300 B.P.)
Social and economic adaptations during this final prehistoric interval in the Antelope Valley
were largely an extension of patterns that developed during the Saratoga Springs period. Trade
along the Mojave River continued to provide the people of the eastern Antelope Valley with a
variety of exotic goods and materials, though trade relationships with coastal groups grew
stronger than trade relationships with groups from the arid interior. Cottonwood Triangular and
Desert Side-notched points were smaller than those derived from previous periods.

Contact/Ethnographic Period (300 B.P.–Present)

This last interval is the period of contact between native desert people and European-American
explorers and settlers. Kroeber (1925) attests that as many as six different native groups were
living in the western Mojave at time of Euro American contact, including the Kawaiisu,
Chemehuevi, Alliklik (Tataviam), Kitanemuk, Vanyume, and Serrano. Blackburn and Bean
(1978) later reinterpreted political geography in the western Mojave, and divided the western
Antelope Valley between the Tataviam (to the south) and the Kitanemuk (to the north). Sutton
(1980:220) followed Blackburn and Bean and claimed that the late prehistoric population in the
majority of Antelope Valley were the ancestors of the ethnographic Kitanemuk. He later
hypothesized that the floor of the valley was abandoned a few decades prior to Spanish contact in
1772 (Sutton 1988; Warren 1984). However, Earle et al. (1997:8) cite the 1772 diary of Pedro
Fages and the 1776 diary of Father Garcés, which mention Indian villages in the western
Antelope Valley to challenge this claim.

The project area lies along the eastern portion of Tataviam territory and the western portion of
Vanyume Serrano territory, north of Fernandeño territory and south of Kitanemuk territory. It is
situated on the “border” of Tataviam and Vanyume Serrano settlement areas and may have been
occupied and used by these groups simultaneously or at different times. These groups are
Shoshonean, and their languages represent Takic branches of the Uto-Aztecan language group.
Inhabitants of the area had access to the resources of the Antelope Valley and to the resources of
the ranges to the east and south. The interface of the two types of biotic zones provided plant and
animal resources that varied with season and elevation. Larger dependence on plant sources for
subsistence is seen in later periods.

A Brief Historic Overview of Antelope Valley and Palmdale History

Settlement and agricultural development began with the completion of the Southern Pacific
Railroad (SPRR) line in the Antelope Valley on September 6, 1876 (Weitze 1993:3). While
sporadic homesteads and grazing stock dotted the Antelope Valley, settlement is attributed to the
mid-1880s land boom in southern California sponsored by various town and colony promoters
(Earle 2003). The SPRR promoted colonizing land near its railroad line, which many immigrants
responded to by founding towns adjacent to the rail line. Today’s Palmdale has its roots in two
small, early communities: Harold (Alpine Station) and Palmenthal.

Establishing railroad stations along the line included the first southern SPRR station in the valley
at Harold, near present-day Barrel Springs Road and Sierra Highway. Harold was a natural
location for a community because it was at the crossroads of the two major routes on the Valley

Anna Choudhari
Page 5 of 20

floor: the Southern Pacific Railroad tracks and Fort Tejon Road (now Barrel Springs Road)
(cityofpalmdaleca.gov n.d.; Serpico 2000:56).

Lancaster, Pennsylvanians established the nearby community of Lancaster in 1877, with
Palmenthal following in 1886 (Weitze 1993:3). Palmenthal was started when land in the
Antelope Valley sold for 50 cents an acre and a group of 50 to 60 Swiss and German Lutheran
families migrated largely from Nebraska and Illinois and settled in the area now known as
Palmdale. They named their new community “Palmenthal” because they had mistaken the native
Joshua trees for the palm trees they had been told to expect to see as they arrived nearer to the
Pacific Ocean (cityofpalmdaleca.gov n.d.; townsquarepublications.com n.d.).

According to Antelope Valley ethnographer David Earle (2003),

  The settlement of the Antelope Valley region was intimately tied up with the
  central role of the San Gabriel Mountains watershed as a water-provider to
  agriculture in southern California. With the experiments of the 1880s aimed at
  developing agricultural specialties of southern California farmers – raisin grapes,
  then almonds, then oranges – the factors of transport facilities and of water
  availability became crucial. From an early date, agriculture in the regions watered
  by the San Gabriel and San Bernardino Mountains watershed was designed to
  serve national and international markets via the rail distribution of specialty
  products such as raisins, nuts, or fruit, products requiring special processing.

Antelope Valley land remained relatively inexpensive and available in the 1880s as part of the
San Gabriel Range watershed. Agricultural colonies developed in proximity to the watercourses
of Big Rock and Littlerock Creek that provided stream runoff for irrigation (Earle 2003). The
emergence of the “California Doctrine” in 1886 as a result of Lux v. Haggin proposed a possible
problem for landowners claiming riparian rights. While the legal decision upheld the riparian
doctrine, in certain instances the prior appropriation doctrine would supersede the riparian
doctrine; landowners in the Antelope Valley that diverted water directly from Little Rock Creek
could find their water rights in jeopardy. The passage of the Wright Act in 1887 intended to
create more opportunities for local farmers by fostering collective water use through the
formation of irrigation districts that could raise revenue and issue bonds, among other authorities
(Earle 2003; Hundley 2001:97-100). A period of wet years (1883-1893) allowed promoters to
advertise the valley as land with plenty of rainfall and underground water, a place where farmers
could practice dry farming and produce grains and tree crops. However, the unusually rainy
period soon ended and a drought followed, which devastated the local economy (Earle 2003).

The towns of Harold and Palmenthal were abandoned as a result of the drought, and the City of
Palmdale was formed in 1899. It remained a small farming community until the mid-twentieth
century, when, with nearby Lancaster, it became a focus for industrial development, chiefly
aircraft assembly and electronic research; in the 1990s, with the rapid economic expansion of
Antelope Valley, it was one of the fastest-growing cities in the United States (Britannica.com
n.d.). The City of Palmdale celebrated its fiftieth anniversary of incorporation on Aug. 24, 2012.

STUDY METHODS

Methods used to assess the presence of and potential for cultural resources within the property
included a search of existing records and a pedestrian field survey. ASM began the study by
requesting a records search from the South Central Coastal Information Center (SCCIC), part of
the California Historical Resources Information System (CHRIS), that included the Project area
and a radius of 1 mile around it. A search of the Sacred Lands File held by the NAHC was also
requested. Historical aerial photographs and USGS topographic maps were assessed to discern
prior land use on the Project parcel.

ASM Senior Archaeologist Sherri Andrews, M.A., RPA conducted an intensive pedestrian
archaeological field survey on September 9, 2023. The survey was undertaken to determine the
presence of any previously undocumented cultural resources that may be discernable on the
surface of the Project parcel using transects spaced at 15-m intervals.

Pedestrian Archaeological Survey

For the archaeological survey, the entire Project parcel was walked in transects spaced
approximately 15 m apart and oriented primarily east/west. The parcel is fairly heavily
vegetated, covered with a number of large stands as well as singular Joshua trees amid juniper
bushes, buckwheat, and creosote, with the balance being covered with low scrub and grasses
(Figures 3 and 4). Surface visibility was variable, with some areas approximately 70-85 percent
and others less than 50 percent. A number of dirt roads traverse the parcel, including a well-used
one that bisects the parcel running roughly north/south (Figure 5). A number of dumping
episodes are evident, especially along the roads and in the northern part of the parcel (Figure 6).
Discarded materials appear to have been brought in from elsewhere as there is no evidence of
any structures having been situated on this or nearby parcels. The dumping episodes likely date
from the 1980s to the present, and include household items, such as mattresses, furniture, carpet,
bottles and cans, degrading lumber, and miscellaneous construction materials and debris.

No previously undocumented cultural resources were encountered during the intensive
pedestrian archaeological survey.

REGULATORY CONTEXT

California Register of Historical Resources (CRHR)

For purposes of CEQA, a historic resource is any object, building, structure, site, area, place,
record, or manuscript listed in or eligible for listing in the CRHR (PRC §5024.1, Title 14 CCR,
§4852). The four criteria for listing in the CRHR closely mirror the criteria for listing in the
NRHP. A resource is eligible for listing in the CRHR if it meets any of the following criteria:

(1)  Is associated with events that have made a significant contribution to the broad patterns
  of California’s history and cultural heritage
(2)  Is associated with the lives of persons important in our past
(3)  Embodies the distinctive characteristics of a type, period, region, or method of
  construction, or represents the work of an important creative individual, or possesses high
  artistic values
(4)  Has yielded, or may be likely to yield, information important to prehistory or history.

Prehistoric archaeological sites are typically evaluated only under Criterion 4 for their potential
to yield data important to understanding the prehistory of the area or region. Historical
archaeological sites and architectural resources may be evaluated under any of the four criteria
because their features, plus available historical documentation, may be used to inform our
understanding of their association with events, people, workmanship, or other important
historical information. Isolates are not eligible for the listing in the CRHR because they lack
association and context with other archaeological materials. Recording the physical description
and location of an isolate exhausts its research potential.

City of Palmdale

The City of Palmdale Municipal Code (PMC) does not include statutes regarding the
preservation of cultural and historic resources. However, the General Plan’s (1993)
Environmental Resources Element includes measures to protect cultural resources, as follows:

GOAL ER7: Protect historical and culturally significant resources which contribute to the
community's sense of history.

Objective ER7.1: Promote the identification and preservation of historic structures, historic sites,
archaeological sites, and paleontological resources in the City.

  •  Policy ER7.1.1: Identify and recognize historic landmarks from Palmdale's past.
  •  Policy ER7.1.2: Promote maintenance, rehabilitation, and appropriate reuse of identified
  landmarks where feasible.
  •  Policy ER7.1.3: Require that new development protect significant historic,
  paleontological, or archaeological resources, or provide for other appropriate mitigation.
  •  Policy ER7.1.4: Develop and maintain a cultural sensitivity map. Require special
  studies/surveys to be prepared for any development proposals in areas reasonably
  suspected of containing cultural resources, or as indicated on the sensitivity map.
  •  Policy ER7.1.5: When human remains, suspected to be of Native American origin are
  discovered, cooperate with the Native American Heritage Commission and any local
  Native American groups to determine the most appropriate disposition of the human
  remains and any associated grave goods.
  •  Policy ER7.1.6: Cooperate with private and public entities whose goals are to protect and
  preserve historic landmarks and important cultural resources.

RECOMMENDATIONS

No prehistoric or historical artifacts or sites were identified during the current survey. As such,
no historical resources as defined under CEQA that would require further consideration were
identified within the Project area. Further, the results of the background research conducted for
the study indicate a low archaeological sensitivity for the Project area.
However, in the event that any archaeological materials are encountered during future
development activities, all activities must be suspended in the vicinity of the find until the
deposits are recorded and evaluated by a qualified archaeologist. If evaluated as eligible for the
CRHR and if impacts to the resource cannot be avoided, mitigation would be necessary. In
addition, if significant subsurface prehistoric resources are encountered that will be subject to
impacts from the project, Tribes with historic and cultural ties to the area shall be contacted.
If human remains of any kind are found during construction, the requirements of CEQA
Guidelines Section 15064.5(e) and AB 2641 shall be followed. According to these requirements,
all construction activities must cease immediately, and the San Bernardino County Coroner and a
qualified archaeologist must be notified. The Coroner will examine the remains and determine
the next appropriate action based on his or her findings. If the coroner determines the remains to
be of Native American origin, he or she will notify the NAHC. The NAHC will then identify the

1.1 General

CMT Technical Services (CMT) was retained to conduct a geotechnical subsurface study for a proposed Maverik
Store. The site for the proposed development is situated at the north side of Avenue S, just west of Highway 14
in Palmdale, California as shown on the Vicinity Map below.

1.2 Objectives, Scope and Authorization

The objectives and scope of our study were planned in communications between Mr. Russ Hamblin of Cardno,
Inc., and Mr. Jeffrey Egbert of CMT. In general, the objectives of this study were to define and evaluate the
subsurface soil and groundwater conditions at the site, and provide appropriate foundation, earthwork,
pavement and seismic recommendations to be utilized in the design and construction of the proposed
development.

In accomplishing these objectives, subsurface explorations consisting of the drilling/logging/sampling of 6 bore
holes, performing an infiltration test in one of the bore holes, and driving a Dynamic Cone Penetrometer (DCP)
at three locations on the site, were performed by Cardno personnel. Our scope of work included performing
laboratory testing on samples of the subsurface soils collected in the bore holes as delivered to us, and

1.3 Description of Proposed Construction

We understand that construction of a new Maverik convenience store and fuel station with accompanying fuel
islands and canopies, and underground fuel storage tanks is planned for the site. We project that wall loads for
the store building will not exceed 4,000 pounds per linear foot. Floor slab loads are anticipated to be relatively
light, with an average uniform loading not exceeding 150 pounds per square foot.

The fuel island canopies will be supported by steel frames and columns extending to the foundation system. It
is projected that the maximum canopy downward column loads will be on the order of 60,000 pounds. In
addition, uplift and lateral loads will be imposed upon these foundations. If the structural loading conditions
are different than we have projected, please notify us so that any appropriate modifications to our conclusions
and recommendations contained herein can be made.

We also understand the parking/drive paved areas will be constructed utilizing both asphalt and concrete
pavement. Concrete pavement will likely be installed in front of the proposed store structure, as well as in the
canopy fuel islands and over the underground storage tank area. In other areas, asphalt concrete sections will
likely be used. Traffic is projected to consist of mostly automobiles and light trucks, a few daily medium-weight
delivery trucks, a weekly garbage truck, and an occasional fire truck. The site plan indicates 76 hi-flow lanes for
which data provided by Maverik indicates up to 200 semi-trucks per day.

The most significant geotechnical aspects regarding site development include the following:

3.  Groundwater was not encountered within the maximum depth explored of about 50 feet.
4.  The site is mapped within a liquefaction zone by the State of California, but the potential for liquefaction
  to occur in the subsurface soils encountered is very low.
5.  An earthquake fault is mapped very near the northeast corner of the site and a fault hazard study may
  be required.
5.  Foundations may be constructed on scarified, re-compacted suitable, natural soils, or on
  structural/engineered fill which extends to scarified, re-compacted natural soils.

  2.0 FIELD EXPLORATION
2.1 General

In order to define and evaluate the subsurface soil and groundwater conditions, 6 bore holes were drilled at the
site to depths of approximately 6.5 to 50.0 feet below the existing ground surface. Locations of the bore holes
are presented on Figure 1 in the Appendix.

Relatively undisturbed samples of the subsurface soils were obtained by driving a split-spoon sampler with 2.05-
inch outside diameter rings/liners into the undisturbed soils below the drill augers. Disturbed samples were
collected utilizing a standard split spoon sampler. The split spoon sampler was driven 18 inches into the soils
below the drill augers using a 140-pound hammer free-falling a distance of 30 inches. The number of hammer
blows needed for each 6-inch interval was recorded. The sum of the hammer blows for the final 12 inches of
penetration is known as a standard penetration test (SPT) and this ‘blow count’ was recorded on the bore hole
logs. Where more than 50 blows occurred before the 6-inch interval was achieved, the sampling was terminated
and the number of blows and inches penetrated by the sampler were recorded. The blow count provides a
reasonable approximation of the relative density of granular soils, but only a limited indication of the relative
consistency of fine-grained soils because the consistency of these soils is significantly influenced by the moisture
content.

The subsurface soil samples retrieved in the bore holes were classified in the field based upon visual and textural
examination in general accordance with ASTM 1 D-2488. These field classifications were supplemented by
subsequent examination and testing of select samples in our laboratory. Graphic logs of the bore holes,
including a description of the soil strata encountered, are presented on the Bore Hole Logs, Figures 2 through
7, included in the Appendix. Sampling information and other pertinent data and observations are also included
on the logs. In addition, a Key to Symbols defining the terms and symbols used on the logs is provided as Figure
8 in the Appendix.

2.2 Infiltration Testing

Infiltration testing was also performed in bore hole B-1 within the natural silt soils. The testing consisted of
drilling to 5 feet below the surface, sampling, removing the sampler, filling the auger with water and measuring
the rate of water drop over approximately 1 hour increments. The final measured rate was approximately 17
minutes per inch. This rate will likely slow over time and an appropriate factor of safety should be applied for
design.

  4.0 GEOLOGIC & SEISMIC CONDITIONS
4.1 Geologic Setting

The subject site is located in the south-central portion of the Antelope Valley at the western tip of the Mojave
Desert Geomorphic Province in southern California. The site sits at an elevation of approximately 2,660 feet
above sea level. The Antelope Valley is a large, flat valley spanning approximately 2,200 square miles. It is
located southeast of the Tehachapi Mountains and Garlock Fault, east of the Sierra Pelona Mountains, and north
of the San Gabriel Mountains and San Andreas Fault, forming a large topographic and groundwater basin
collecting water runoff from the surrounding mountains. Human use such as long-term groundwater pumping
has lowered the water table, resulting in land subsidence and drop in elevation of the basin over time.

During the history of the Antelope Valley region, a large intermittent lake formed near the center of the basin
and deposited various types of fine-grained sediment based on precipitation. Significant precipitation sourced
massive beds of blue clay formed in a deep perennial lake, while mild precipitation deposited thin beds of clay

and evaporate salt deposits formed in playas or shallow intermittent lakes. The clay yields little to no water to
wells, but the interbedded, coarser material can yield considerable volumes of water. Soils within the area are
derived from loess and alluvial material sourced from granitic rock and others originating along the slopes of
the Tehachapi and San Gabriel Mountains that were shed into the valley.

The geology of CGS Ritter Ridge 7.5’ quadrangle, Los Angeles County, California, which includes the location of
the subject site, has been mapped by Hernandez 2. The surficial geology of the subject site and adjacent
properties is mapped as “Modern alluvium” (map unit Qa) dated to be Holocene. Unit Qa is described in the
referenced mapping as “Unconsolidated to weakly consolidated, mostly undissected, fluvial gravel, sand, and
silt. Loose, yellowish-grey sand, silt, and pebble-cobble gravel. Consists predominantly of moderately sorted
coarse-grained to very coarse-grained arkosic sand.” No fill has been recorded at the location of the site on the

4.3 Seismicity
4.3.1 Site Class

We understand that the State of California Building Code (SCBC) 2019 was adopted on January 1, 2020, which
we anticipate will be the code for design of the structures at this site. SCBC 2019 refers to Chapter 20, Site
Classification Procedure for Seismic Design, of ASCE 4 7-16, which stipulates that the average values of shear
wave velocity, blow count and/or shear strength within the upper 100 feet (30 meters) be utilized to determine
seismic site class. Based on the SPT blow counts obtained in bore hole B-1, which extended approximately 50
feet below the surface, and projecting that subsurface soils to 100 feet will be similar, it is our opinion the site
best fits Site Class D – Stiff Soil (with data), which we recommend for seismic structural design.

4.3.3 Liquefaction

Liquefaction is defined as the condition when saturated, loose, sandy soils lose their support capabilities
because of excessive pore water pressure which develops during a seismic event. Clayey soils, even if saturated,
will generally not liquefy during a major seismic event.

The previously referenced California Geological Survey mapping indicates the site is within a liquefaction zone.
Groundwater was not encountered to the maximum depth explored of approximately 50 feet below the existing
ground surface. Given these conditions, liquefaction will not occur at the site in the soils encountered.

4.4 Other Geologic Hazards

The site is not located within a known or mapped potential debris flow, stream flooding5, or rock fall hazard
area. No landslide deposits or features, including lateral spread deposits, are mapped on or adjacent to the site.

  6.0 SITE PREPARATION AND GRADING
6.1 General

All deleterious materials should be stripped from the site prior to commencement of construction activities.
This includes vegetation, topsoil, loose and disturbed soils, etc. Topsoil approximately 12 inches in thickness
was noted on the surface at the bore hole locations. When stripping and grubbing, topsoil should be
distinguished by the apparent organic content and not solely by color; thus, we estimate that topsoil stripping
will need to include at least the upper 6 inches, but roots may locally extend deeper.

Fill placed over large areas to raise overall site grades can induce settlements in the underlying natural soils. If
more than 3 feet of site grading fill is anticipated over the existing ground surface, we should be notified to
assess potential settlements and provide additional recommendations as needed. These recommendations may
include placement of the site grading fill far in advance to allow potential settlements to occur prior to
construction.

6.2 Temporary Excavations

Excavations up to 16 feet deep for underground fuel storage tanks are anticipated at the site. Based upon bore
hole B-6 it appears that excavations at the proposed tank pit location will encounter mostly silt.

6.5 Utility Trenches

For the bedding zone around the utility, we recommend utilizing sand bedding fill material that meets current
local or APWA 7 requirements.

All utility trench backfill material below structurally loaded facilities (foundations, floor slabs, flatwork, parking

Most utility companies and local governments are requiring Type A-1a or A-1b (AASHTO Designation) soils

6.6 Stabilization

To stabilize soft subgrade conditions a mixture of coarse, clean, angular gravels and cobbles and/or 1.5- to 2.0-
inch clean gravel should be utilized. Often the amount of gravelly material can be reduced with the use of a
geotextile fabric such as Mirafi RS280i, or equivalent. Its use will also help avoid mixing of the subgrade soils
with the gravelly material. After excavating the soft/disturbed soils, the fabric should be spread across the
bottom of the excavation and up the sides a minimum of 18 inches. Otherwise, it should be placed in accordance
with the manufacturer’s recommendation, including proper overlaps. The gravel material can then be placed
over the fabric in compacted lifts as described above.

  7.0 FOUNDATION RECOMMENDATIONS
The following recommendations have been developed on the basis of the previously described project
characteristics, the subsurface conditions observed in the field and the laboratory test data, as well as common
geotechnical engineering practice.

7.1 Foundation Recommendations

Based on our geotechnical engineering analyses, the proposed structures may be supported upon conventional
spread and/or continuous wall foundations placed on suitable, scarified and re-compacted natural soils, or on
structural fill placed on suitable, scarified, re-compacted natural soils. Footings may be designed using a net
bearing pressure of 2,000 psf if bearing on scarified and re-compacted natural soils, and 2,500 psf if bearing on a
minimum of 18 inches of structural fill placed upon scarified, re-compacted natural soils. The term “net bearing
pressure” refers to the pressure imposed by the portion of the structure located above lowest adjacent final grade,
thus the weight of the footing and backfill to lowest adjacent final grade need not be considered. The allowable
bearing pressure may be increased by 1/3 for temporary loads such as wind and seismic forces.

We also recommend the following:

1.  Exterior footings subject to frost should be placed at least 18 inches below final grade, or per city standards
  if deeper.
2.  Interior footings not subject to frost should be placed at least 12 inches below grade.
3.  Continuous footing widths should be maintained at a minimum of 18 inches.
4.  Spot footings should be a minimum of 24 inches wide.

7.2 Installation

Under no circumstances shall foundations be placed on undocumented fill, topsoil with organics, sod, rubbish,
construction debris, other deleterious materials, frozen soils, or within ponded water. If unsuitable soils are
encountered, they must be completely removed and replaced with properly compacted structural fill. The base
of footing excavations and floor slab sub grades should be observed by a qualified geotechnical engineer to
confirm that suitable bearing soils have been exposed.
 Geotechnical Engineering Study  Page 12
Proposed Maverik Store, Palmdale, CA
Project No. 18988

The base of footing excavations should be scarified a minimum of 12 inches, moisture conditioned as needed, and
re-compacted to the requirements for structural fill given in Section 6.4 prior to forming for footings or placement
of structural fill.

All structural fill should meet the requirements for such, and should be placed and compacted in accordance with
Section 6 above. The width of structural replacement fill below footings should be equal to the width of the
footing plus 1 foot for each foot of fill thickness. For instance, if the footing width is 2 feet and the structural fill
depth beneath the footing is 4 feet, the fill replacement width should be 6 feet, centered beneath the footing.

The minimum thickness of structural fill below footings should be equivalent to one-third the thickness of
structural fill below any other portion of the foundations. For example, if the maximum depth of structural fill is
6 feet, all footings for the new structure should be underlain by a minimum 2 feet of structural fill.

7.3 Estimated Settlement

Foundations designed and constructed in accordance with our recommendations could experience some
settlement, but we anticipate that total settlements of footings founded as recommended above will not exceed
1 inch, with differential settlements on the order of 0.5 inches over a distance of 25 feet. We expect
approximately 50% of the total settlement to initially take place during construction.

7.4 Lateral Resistance

Lateral loads imposed upon foundations due to wind or seismic forces may be resisted by the development of
passive earth pressures and friction between the base of the footings and the supporting soils. In determining
frictional resistance, a coefficient of 0.30 for natural soils and 0.40 for structural fill may be utilized for design.
Passive resistance provided by properly placed and compacted natural soils above the water table may be
considered equivalent to a fluid with a density of 350 pcf. A combination of passive earth resistance and friction
may be utilized if the passive pressure component of the total is divided by 1.5.

7.5 Uplift Loads

Uplift loads may be resisted by the weight of the foundation and the backfill wedge above the top of the
foundation within the area defined by an imaginary line extending outward from the outside top edge of the
footing 10 degrees from vertical, up to final grade. A unit weight of 120 pounds per square foot can be used for
sand and gravel backfill over the footings.

  9.0 BOUYANT FORCES
Groundwater was not encountered to the maximum depth explored of 50 feet. Based upon this condition we
anticipate that underground tanks will not need to be designed to resist buoyant forces.

  10.0 FLOOR SLABS
Floor slabs may be established upon suitable, natural scarified and re-compacted soils and/or on structural fill
extending to suitable, natural scarified and re-compacted soils (same as for foundations). Under no
circumstances shall floor slabs be established directly on any topsoil, undocumented fills, loose or disturbed
soils, sod, rubbish, construction debris, other deleterious materials, frozen soils, or within ponded water.

In order to facilitate curing of the concrete, we recommend that floor slabs be directly underlain by at least 4
inches of “free-draining” fill, such as “pea” gravel or 3/4-inch quarters to 1-inch minus, clean, gap-graded gravel.
To help control normal shrinkage and stress cracking, the floor slabs should have the following features:

  1. Adequate reinforcement for the anticipated floor loads with the reinforcement continuous through
  interior floor joints;
  2. Frequent crack control joints; and
  3. Non-rigid attachment of the slabs to foundation walls and bearing slabs.

  11.0 DRAINAGE RECOMMENDATIONS
It is important to the long-term performance of foundations and floor slabs that water not be allowed to collect
near the foundation walls and infiltrate into the underlying soils. We recommend the following:

1.  All areas around the structures should be sloped to provide drainage away from the foundations. We
  recommend a minimum slope of 4 inches in the first 10 feet away from the structure. This slope should
  be maintained throughout the lifetime of the structure.

2.  All roof drainage should be collected in rain gutters with downspouts designed to discharge at least 10 feet
  from the foundation walls or well beyond the backfill limits, whichever is greater.

3.  Adequate compaction of the foundation backfill should be provided. We suggest a minimum of 90% of
  the maximum laboratory density as determined by ASTM D-698. Water consolidation methods should not
  be used under any circumstances.

4.  Landscape sprinklers should be aimed away from foundation walls. The sprinkling systems should be
  designed with proper drainage and be well-maintained. Over watering should be avoided.

5.  Other precautions that may become evident during construction.

  12.0 PAVEMENTS
All pavement areas must be prepared as discussed above in Section 6.1. Under no circumstances shall
pavements be established over topsoil, un-prepared existing undocumented fill soils, loose or disturbed soils,
sod, rubbish, construction debris, other deleterious materials, frozen soils, or within ponded water.

To assess subgrade strength for pavement support Dynamic Cone Penetrometer (DCP) tests were performed at
three locations within proposed pavement areas. Test results were varied, with correlated average California
Bearing Ratio (CBR) values ranging from 4.3 to 9.1 (see Figures 11 through 13). We have utilized a correlated
CBR value of 5 as the basis for the pavement design.

  13.0 QUALITY CONTROL
We recommend that a comprehensive quality control testing and observation program be established during
construction to help facilitate implementation of our recommendations and address, in a timely manner, any
subsurface conditions encountered which vary from those described in this report. Without such a program
CMT cannot be responsible for application of our recommendations to subsurface conditions which may vary
from those described herein. This program may include, but not necessarily be limited to, the following:

13.1 Field Observations

Observations should be completed during all phases of construction such as site preparation, foundation
excavation, structural fill placement and concrete placement.

13.2 Fill Compaction

Compaction testing is required for all structural supporting fill materials. Maximum Dry Density (Standard
Proctor, ASTM D-698) tests should be requested by the contractor immediately after delivery of any fill
materials. The maximum density information should then be used for field density tests on each lift as necessary
to ensure that the required compaction is being achieved.

13.3 Excavations

All excavation procedures and processes should be observed by a geotechnical engineer. In addition, for the

designations.

  14.0 LIMITATIONS

become necessary to re-evaluate the recommendations of this report after we have observed the variation.

 I.  PURPOSE AND SCOPE

This report was prepared in support of the Maverik Fueling Station Palmdale Entitlement package.
The purpose of this report is to analyze the existing and proposed drainage patterns, discuss the
on-site drainage design and size the proposed on-site drainage facilities in order to meet the City
of Palmdale and County of Los Angeles Public Department of Works requirements.

The proposed project involves the development of an 8,852 square-foot gas station and attached
convenience store and quick service restaurant located at the northwest corner of Avenue S and
State Route 14 (APN 3004-016-032), City of Palmdale, Los Angeles County, California. The
subject parcel is currently undeveloped and 100% pervious in its current condition. The site is
bound to the south fully improved public streets; however, there are no public storm drain facilities
in this area.

In general, the existing site is not subject to offsite storm flows and there is no existing onsite
retention of storm flow. The project proposes to obtain access from Avenue S to the south for
access onto the site. The site area drains from northeast to the southwest under the existing and
proposed conditions.

The proposed impervious area is 77,285 square-feet (1.77 acres). The new improvements will
include six fueling station islands, convenience store, quick service restaurant, and outdoor patio
area. Two on-site stormwater retention basins will be constructed to collect and store storm runoff
generated during the 25-year design storm per City of Palmdale drainage requirements. One basin
will be located along the southwesterly property boundary; the second basin will be located along
the southerly property boundary.
 II.  DESIGN METHODOLOGY AND SITE CONDITIONS

The 5.91 acre existing site where improvements are proposed is currently undeveloped. The site
is located in an area consisting of sandy soils that exhibited a moderate infiltration rate during
testing. The terrain slopes mildly from the northeast corner to the southwest corner of the lot. In
general, the existing site is not subject to offsite storm flows. In the developed condition, less than
half of the project site will be paved surfaces.

The project will provide an on-site storm drain system designed to capture the runoff generated
from a 25-year, 24-hour design storm based on existing undeveloped conditions per the City of
Palmdale drainage requirements. Two separate storm retention systems will be proposed to
capture, store, and infiltrate the on-site runoff generated during the design storm event. Runoff
from the convenience store rooftop and fueling station canopies will be captured and included in
the runoff volume conveyed to the retention systems. However, no rainfall will be allowed to land
on the portion of the fueling station island where there is a potential for pollutant spills and cleanup.
These areas are protected from rainfall by the overhead canopies. Additionally, a swale drain
system will be implemented to capture surface flows from the fueling islands and conveyed to a
separate oil separator system located onsite. Overflow from the oil separator system will be
connected to the site’s sewer septic system to prevent pollutants from co-mingling with storm
runoff that could potentially enter into an MS4 facility as required by the National Pollution
Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permit. Overflow of pollution elimination systems is
generally directed sewer septic rather than infiltration type storm drain facilities in order to prevent
potential for soil contamination by pollutants. Conveyance of possible fuel and oil spills via the
oil separator that connects to the sewer septic system because it is less likely to leave the site with
storm runoff during the overflow condition.

On-site tested infiltration rates are 3.53 in/hr and an assumed infiltration rate of 3 in/hr will be used
for design purposes to provide a Factor of Safety. Per City of Palmdale requirements, the
preliminary hydrology calculations will be per the method outlined in the Los Angeles County
Hydrology Manual – Section 3 Storm Drain Hydrology – to quantify the runoff volume generated
and stored on-site during the design storm return period. Infiltration of stored runoff is assumed to
occur on the bottom of the on-site retention system. The Los Angeles County Soil Types GIS
database was used to determine the site soil type.

Pre-Developed Conditions

On-Site:

The existing onsite conditions is considered as a single subarea because the entire site drains from
the northeast corner of the property boundary to the southwest corner. The site lies within Zone
“X” according to FEMA Map No. 06037C0670F, dated 9/26/2008 (Appendix D). Zone “X” is
identified as an area of minimal flood hazard with a 1% chance flood – depth 1 foot or less –
annually. The site has no existing drainage structures and all runoff is conveyed via sheet flow.
The conveyed flow leaves the site and flows southerly along Guoyan Avenue. Refer to appendices
for HydroCalc results. Refer to table below for summary calculations:

Determine the SWQDv

The design storm for the proposed project location is 0.75‐inch, 24‐hour rain event. Using the
HydroCalc program provided by the Los Angeles County Department of Public Works, the
stormwater quality design volume (SWQDv) was calculated with the characteristics above.

Under pre‐development conditions, the required 24‐hour clear runoff volume is 2,873 cu‐ft.
Under post development conditions, the 24‐hour clear runoff volume is 5,413 cu‐ft. Therefore,
the ∆SWQDv is 2,540 cu‐ft.

See attached for HydroCalc data and related hydrographs.

Determine the Design Infiltration Rate

Submitted herewith is the report of our geotechnical engineering study for the subject site. This report contains the results
of our findings and an engineering interpretation of the results with respect to the available project characteristics. It also
contains recommendations to aid in the design and construction of the earth-related phases of this project.

On August 26, 2022, Cardno personnel were onsite and supervised the drilling of 6 bore holes at the site extending to
depths between about 6.5 and 50.0 feet below the existing ground surface. Soil samples were obtained in the bore holes
during the field operations and subsequently transported to our laboratory for further testing and observation.

Natural subsurface soils consisted of SILT (ML) and SAND (SM). Groundwater was not encountered in the explorations.
Based upon the results of our study the proposed structures may be supported on conventional strip and spread footings
founded on suitable, undisturbed, natural sand soils, or on structural fill placed on suitable, undisturbed natural soils. A
detailed discussion of design and construction criteria is presented in this report.

  1.0 INTRODUCTION
1.1 General

CMT Technical Services (CMT) was retained to conduct a geotechnical subsurface study for a proposed Maverik
Store. The site for the proposed development is situated at the north side of Avenue S, just west of Highway 14
in Palmdale, California as shown on the Vicinity Map below.

  VICINITY MAP

1.2 Objectives, Scope and Authorization

The objectives and scope of our study were planned in communications between Mr. Russ Hamblin of Cardno,
Inc., and Mr. Jeffrey Egbert of CMT. In general, the objectives of this study were to define and evaluate the
subsurface soil and groundwater conditions at the site, and provide appropriate foundation, earthwork,
pavement and seismic recommendations to be utilized in the design and construction of the proposed
development.

In accomplishing these objectives, subsurface explorations consisting of the drilling/logging/sampling of 6 bore
holes, performing an infiltration test in one of the bore holes, and driving a Dynamic Cone Penetrometer (DCP)
at three locations on the site, were performed by Cardno personnel. Our scope of work included performing
laboratory testing on samples of the subsurface soils collected in the bore holes as delivered to us, and

1.3 Description of Proposed Construction

We understand that construction of a new Maverik convenience store and fuel station with accompanying fuel
islands and canopies, and underground fuel storage tanks is planned for the site. We project that wall loads for
the store building will not exceed 4,000 pounds per linear foot. Floor slab loads are anticipated to be relatively
light, with an average uniform loading not exceeding 150 pounds per square foot.

The fuel island canopies will be supported by steel frames and columns extending to the foundation system. It
is projected that the maximum canopy downward column loads will be on the order of 60,000 pounds. In
addition, uplift and lateral loads will be imposed upon these foundations. If the structural loading conditions
are different than we have projected, please notify us so that any appropriate modifications to our conclusions
and recommendations contained herein can be made.

We also understand the parking/drive paved areas will be constructed utilizing both asphalt and concrete
pavement. Concrete pavement will likely be installed in front of the proposed store structure, as well as in the
canopy fuel islands and over the underground storage tank area. In other areas, asphalt concrete sections will
likely be used. Traffic is projected to consist of mostly automobiles and light trucks, a few daily medium-weight
delivery trucks, a weekly garbage truck, and an occasional fire truck. The site plan indicates 76 hi-flow lanes for
which data provided by Maverik indicates up to 200 semi-trucks per day.

1.4 Executive Summary

The most significant geotechnical aspects regarding site development include the following:

1.  Moderate vegetation, including large shrubs and small trees, and topsoil to be removed.
2.  Subsurface natural soils generally consisted of near surface SILT (ML) layers, followed by SAND (SM).
3.  Groundwater was not encountered within the maximum depth explored of about 50 feet.
4.  The site is mapped within a liquefaction zone by the State of California, but the potential for liquefaction
  to occur in the subsurface soils encountered is very low.
5.  An earthquake fault is mapped very near the northeast corner of the site and a fault hazard study may
  be required.
5.  Foundations may be constructed on scarified, re-compacted suitable, natural soils, or on
  structural/engineered fill which extends to scarified, re-compacted natural soils.

A qualified geotechnical engineer must assess that undocumented fill (if encountered), topsoil, debris, disturbed
or unsuitable soils have been removed and that suitable soils have been encountered prior to placing
structural/site grading fills, footings, slabs, and pavements.

  2.0 FIELD EXPLORATION
2.1 General

In order to define and evaluate the subsurface soil and groundwater conditions, 6 bore holes were drilled at the
site to depths of approximately 6.5 to 50.0 feet below the existing ground surface. Locations of the bore holes
are presented on Figure 1 in the Appendix.

Relatively undisturbed samples of the subsurface soils were obtained by driving a split-spoon sampler with 2.05-
inch outside diameter rings/liners into the undisturbed soils below the drill augers. Disturbed samples were
collected utilizing a standard split spoon sampler. The split spoon sampler was driven 18 inches into the soils
below the drill augers using a 140-pound hammer free-falling a distance of 30 inches. The number of hammer
blows needed for each 6-inch interval was recorded. The sum of the hammer blows for the final 12 inches of
penetration is known as a standard penetration test (SPT) and this ‘blow count’ was recorded on the bore hole
logs. Where more than 50 blows occurred before the 6-inch interval was achieved, the sampling was terminated
and the number of blows and inches penetrated by the sampler were recorded. The blow count provides a
reasonable approximation of the relative density of granular soils, but only a limited indication of the relative
consistency of fine-grained soils because the consistency of these soils is significantly influenced by the moisture
content.

The subsurface soil samples retrieved in the bore holes were classified in the field based upon visual and textural
examination in general accordance with ASTM 1 D-2488. These field classifications were supplemented by
subsequent examination and testing of select samples in our laboratory. Graphic logs of the bore holes,
including a description of the soil strata encountered, are presented on the Bore Hole Logs, Figures 2 through
7, included in the Appendix. Sampling information and other pertinent data and observations are also included
on the logs. In addition, a Key to Symbols defining the terms and symbols used on the logs is provided as Figure
8 in the Appendix.

2.2 Infiltration Testing

Infiltration testing was also performed in bore hole B-1 within the natural silt soils. The testing consisted of
drilling to 5 feet below the surface, sampling, removing the sampler, filling the auger with water and measuring
the rate of water drop over approximately 1 hour increments. The final measured rate was approximately 17
minutes per inch. This rate will likely slow over time and an appropriate factor of safety should be applied for
design.

  4.0 GEOLOGIC & SEISMIC CONDITIONS
4.1 Geologic Setting

The subject site is located in the south-central portion of the Antelope Valley at the western tip of the Mojave
Desert Geomorphic Province in southern California. The site sits at an elevation of approximately 2,660 feet
above sea level. The Antelope Valley is a large, flat valley spanning approximately 2,200 square miles. It is
located southeast of the Tehachapi Mountains and Garlock Fault, east of the Sierra Pelona Mountains, and north
of the San Gabriel Mountains and San Andreas Fault, forming a large topographic and groundwater basin
collecting water runoff from the surrounding mountains. Human use such as long-term groundwater pumping
has lowered the water table, resulting in land subsidence and drop in elevation of the basin over time.

During the history of the Antelope Valley region, a large intermittent lake formed near the center of the basin
and deposited various types of fine-grained sediment based on precipitation. Significant precipitation sourced
massive beds of blue clay formed in a deep perennial lake, while mild precipitation deposited thin beds of clay

the Tehachapi and San Gabriel Mountains that were shed into the valley.

The geology of CGS Ritter Ridge 7.5’ quadrangle, Los Angeles County, California, which includes the location of

4.3 Seismicity
4.3.1 Site Class

We understand that the State of California Building Code (SCBC) 2019 was adopted on January 1, 2020, which
we anticipate will be the code for design of the structures at this site. SCBC 2019 refers to Chapter 20, Site
Classification Procedure for Seismic Design, of ASCE 4 7-16, which stipulates that the average values of shear
wave velocity, blow count and/or shear strength within the upper 100 feet (30 meters) be utilized to determine
seismic site class. Based on the SPT blow counts obtained in bore hole B-1, which extended approximately 50
feet below the surface, and projecting that subsurface soils to 100 feet will be similar, it is our opinion the site
best fits Site Class D – Stiff Soil (with data), which we recommend for seismic structural design.

4.3.3 Liquefaction

Liquefaction is defined as the condition when saturated, loose, sandy soils lose their support capabilities
because of excessive pore water pressure which develops during a seismic event. Clayey soils, even if saturated,
will generally not liquefy during a major seismic event.

The previously referenced California Geological Survey mapping indicates the site is within a liquefaction zone.
Groundwater was not encountered to the maximum depth explored of approximately 50 feet below the existing
ground surface. Given these conditions, liquefaction will not occur at the site in the soils encountered.

4.4 Other Geologic Hazards

The site is not located within a known or mapped potential debris flow, stream flooding5, or rock fall hazard
area. No landslide deposits or features, including lateral spread deposits, are mapped on or adjacent to the site.

  5.0 SITE CONDITIONS
5.1 Surface Conditions

At the time the bore holes were drilled, the site was vacant land moderately vegetated with weeds, brush, and
some cactus. Site grades sloped downward to the south. Based on aerial photos dating back to 1995 that are
readily available on the internet, the site appears to have been vacant since that time. The site is bordered on
the north, east, and west by similar vacant land, and on the south by Avenue S (see Vicinity Map in Section 1.1
above).

5.2 Subsurface Soils

Topsoil approximately 12 inches in thickness was noted on the surface at the bore hole locations. Subsurface
natural soils encountered predominately consisted of near surface layers of red-yellow, slightly moist Sandy SILT
(ML), and occasionally Sandy SILTY CLAY (CL-ML), extending to the bottom of bore holes B-1 through B-5, and
to about 15 feet below the surface in B-6. Based upon the SPT blow counts these soils have stiff to hard
consistency. Below the silt in B-6 a layer of brown, slightly moist Silty SAND (SM), with varying amounts of
gravel, was encountered which extended to about 40 feet below the surface. Blow counts indicate the sand is
very dense. At about 40 feet the soils turned predominately silty again and were hard based on the blow counts,
extending to the bottom of B-6 at about 50 feet below the surface.

5.3 Groundwater

Groundwater was not encountered within the maximum depth explored of 50 feet below the existing surface.

5.4 Site Subsurface Variations

Based on the results of the subsurface explorations and our experience, variations in the continuity and nature
of subsurface conditions should be anticipated. Due to the heterogeneous characteristics of natural soils, care
should be taken in interpolating or extrapolating subsurface conditions between or beyond the exploratory
locations.

  6.0 SITE PREPARATION AND GRADING
6.1 General

All deleterious materials should be stripped from the site prior to commencement of construction activities.
This includes vegetation, topsoil, loose and disturbed soils, etc. Topsoil approximately 12 inches in thickness
was noted on the surface at the bore hole locations. When stripping and grubbing, topsoil should be
distinguished by the apparent organic content and not solely by color; thus, we estimate that topsoil stripping
will need to include at least the upper 6 inches, but roots may locally extend deeper.

Fill placed over large areas to raise overall site grades can induce settlements in the underlying natural soils. If
more than 3 feet of site grading fill is anticipated over the existing ground surface, we should be notified to
assess potential settlements and provide additional recommendations as needed. These recommendations may
include placement of the site grading fill far in advance to allow potential settlements to occur prior to
construction.

6.2 Temporary Excavations

Excavations up to 16 feet deep for underground fuel storage tanks are anticipated at the site. Based upon bore
hole B-6 it appears that excavations at the proposed tank pit location will encounter mostly silt.

For the bedding zone around the utility, we recommend utilizing sand bedding fill material that meets current

6.6 Stabilization

To stabilize soft subgrade conditions a mixture of coarse, clean, angular gravels and cobbles and/or 1.5- to 2.0-
inch clean gravel should be utilized. Often the amount of gravelly material can be reduced with the use of a
geotextile fabric such as Mirafi RS280i, or equivalent. Its use will also help avoid mixing of the subgrade soils
with the gravelly material. After excavating the soft/disturbed soils, the fabric should be spread across the
bottom of the excavation and up the sides a minimum of 18 inches. Otherwise, it should be placed in accordance
with the manufacturer’s recommendation, including proper overlaps. The gravel material can then be placed
over the fabric in compacted lifts as described above.

  7.0 FOUNDATION RECOMMENDATIONS
The following recommendations have been developed on the basis of the previously described project
characteristics, the subsurface conditions observed in the field and the laboratory test data, as well as common
geotechnical engineering practice.

7.1 Foundation Recommendations

Based on our geotechnical engineering analyses, the proposed structures may be supported upon conventional
spread and/or continuous wall foundations placed on suitable, scarified and re-compacted natural soils, or on
structural fill placed on suitable, scarified, re-compacted natural soils. Footings may be designed using a net
bearing pressure of 2,000 psf if bearing on scarified and re-compacted natural soils, and 2,500 psf if bearing on a
minimum of 18 inches of structural fill placed upon scarified, re-compacted natural soils. The term “net bearing
pressure” refers to the pressure imposed by the portion of the structure located above lowest adjacent final grade,
thus the weight of the footing and backfill to lowest adjacent final grade need not be considered. The allowable
bearing pressure may be increased by 1/3 for temporary loads such as wind and seismic forces.

We also recommend the following:

1.  Exterior footings subject to frost should be placed at least 18 inches below final grade, or per city standards
  if deeper.
2.  Interior footings not subject to frost should be placed at least 12 inches below grade.
3.  Continuous footing widths should be maintained at a minimum of 18 inches.
4.  Spot footings should be a minimum of 24 inches wide.

7.2 Installation

Under no circumstances shall foundations be placed on undocumented fill, topsoil with organics, sod, rubbish,
construction debris, other deleterious materials, frozen soils, or within ponded water. If unsuitable soils are
encountered, they must be completely removed and replaced with properly compacted structural fill. The base
of footing excavations and floor slab sub grades should be observed by a qualified geotechnical engineer to
confirm that suitable bearing soils have been exposed.

The minimum thickness of structural fill below footings should be equivalent to one-third the thickness of
structural fill below any other portion of the foundations. For example, if the maximum depth of structural fill is
6 feet, all footings for the new structure should be underlain by a minimum 2 feet of structural fill.

7.3 Estimated Settlement

Foundations designed and constructed in accordance with our recommendations could experience some
settlement, but we anticipate that total settlements of footings founded as recommended above will not exceed
1 inch, with differential settlements on the order of 0.5 inches over a distance of 25 feet. We expect
approximately 50% of the total settlement to initially take place during construction.

7.4 Lateral Resistance

Lateral loads imposed upon foundations due to wind or seismic forces may be resisted by the development of
passive earth pressures and friction between the base of the footings and the supporting soils. In determining
frictional resistance, a coefficient of 0.30 for natural soils and 0.40 for structural fill may be utilized for design.
Passive resistance provided by properly placed and compacted natural soils above the water table may be
considered equivalent to a fluid with a density of 350 pcf. A combination of passive earth resistance and friction
may be utilized if the passive pressure component of the total is divided by 1.5.

7.5 Uplift Loads

Uplift loads may be resisted by the weight of the foundation and the backfill wedge above the top of the
foundation within the area defined by an imaginary line extending outward from the outside top edge of the
footing 10 degrees from vertical, up to final grade. A unit weight of 120 pounds per square foot can be used for
sand and gravel backfill over the footings.
